units.text: The clock above the concourse reads 1954 in its bones — poured concrete, broad canopy, that postwar confidence that rail would carry the nation forward forever. New Orleans Union Passenger Terminal replaced six separate depots that once scattered passengers across the city. The Illinois Central alone had its own house here; now we share the same platform with the Crescent and the City of New Orleans. The train we're on is headed north on one of the most storied rail corridors in America — the IC main line, the track that generations called simply the Panama Limited route. We're rolling now.

Underneath us — right now, and for the next fifty miles — the earth is almost entirely young. Cenozoic rock: the broad category for everything laid down in the last 66 million years, after the dinosaurs cleared the stage. Here in the Mississippi Alluvial Plain, that means sediment that arrived by water, grain by grain, flood by flood. The Mississippi River built this land. It built Orleans Parish. It built the floor beneath this station. The river still adjusts its meanders seasonally, still deposits fine silt on the floodplain after every high water. We're riding across a landscape that is, in geologic terms, barely finished.

The Mississippi Alluvial Plain is the biome we're in — a vast, low, flat province of river-deposited soils stretching from southern Illinois to the Gulf. It is extraordinarily fertile and extraordinarily wet. The alluvium here runs deep. Drive a post into the ground anywhere in New Orleans and you are driving it into sediment that the river carried from Montana and Minnesota and Ohio, mixed and sorted and dropped here over millions of years. The city floats on it, essentially. So does everything we'll see until we climb, slowly, onto higher ground north of mile fifty.

To our right, the Pontchartrain Center — a modest arena that opened in 1991, hosting concerts and hockey and the ordinary civic life of Kenner, Jefferson Parish's largest community. Jefferson Parish wraps around New Orleans on the west and south; it's the suburban ring, more prosperous on average than Orleans, and it sits on the same alluvial floor. The parish seat is Gretna, across the river. We pass through the edge of this suburban landscape quickly — subdivisions, a warehouse district, the geometry of a mid-century American suburb pressed up against an ancient river delta.

The Illinois Central Railroad — the line beneath our wheels — was platted and built in the 1850s, and by the 1860s it ran from Chicago to Cairo, Illinois, where it connected south toward the Gulf. It became the arterial corridor for what historians call the Great Migration: roughly six million Black Americans who left the rural South between 1910 and 1970, riding trains like this one north toward Chicago, Detroit, Cleveland. The IC was not the only route, but it was among the most traveled.

Think about what that means geographically. The train left from towns we'll pass through in the next hour — from parishes like this one, from the sugarcane fields of St. John the Baptist, from the small cities of the Mississippi interior. It arrived, sixty or so hours later, in Chicago. The same distance by foot would have taken weeks. The railroad compressed it into a single night and a day. Families who had never left their county could, for a few dollars, step into a different world. That compression — geographic, economic, social — is part of what made the Migration so rapid and so transformative. We're traveling its southern end right now, moving north on the same right-of-way.

Out the left window: Norco. The name derives from New Orleans Refining Company — the plant that has dominated this town since the early twentieth century. Today it's a Shell and Valero complex, one of the larger petrochemical facilities on the lower Mississippi. The river we've been tracking since New Orleans curves close here, and the refineries sit on its bank for the same reason the sugar plantations did a century earlier: river access, flat land, proximity to transportation. The geology that laid down this alluvial plain also concentrated the organic material — ancient sea life, compressed over millions of years — that eventually became the oil and gas now processed at facilities like this one.

Cancer Alley, some call this stretch of the river between New Orleans and Baton Rouge. Eighty miles of petrochemical plants and the communities that live alongside them. The air quality data for St. Charles Parish puts it among the highest industrial pollution exposures in the country. The people who live in Norco — population just under three thousand — are the descendants of the same labor that worked these riverbanks when the commodity was cane sugar rather than crude oil. The crop changed. The economic structure did not change much at all.

St. John the Baptist Parish begins around mile twenty-four, and it is — according to the land cover data — one hundred percent wetland. Every acre. The parish seat is Edgard, an unincorporated cluster on the west bank. The largest community is LaPlace, on the east bank where we're traveling. What you're seeing out the windows now, if you look away from the industrial corridor, is what the lower Mississippi always looked like before drainage and levees: cypress swamp, standing water, floating mats of vegetation, the occasional heron working a shallow ditch.

Sugarcane has been grown here since the colonial period. The crop survives in St. John the Baptist Parish, though only as a fragment of the plantation economy that once covered these bottoms. Cane requires a frost-free growing season — this far south, the climate just barely allows it. Every degree of latitude north we travel over the next hour makes cane cultivation less viable. By the time we reach Hammond, we're at the edge of cane country. Beyond that, it's a different agricultural world.

Ahead and to either side, the land opens into one of the stranger crossings on this route. The Manchac Swamp Bridge — that's the highway structure you can see in the distance, carrying Interstate 55 and U.S. Route 51 over the swamp on concrete pilings — was completed in 1979. It is miles long. The swamp it crosses is the backwater between Lake Pontchartrain and Lake Maurepas, two broad, shallow lakes connected by the Manchac Pass.

We cross the swamp on a rail trestle that predates the highway bridge by decades. The Illinois Central laid track through here in the railroad's great expansion era; the engineers had no good options — the swamp had to be bridged or crossed on fill, and fill in this terrain sinks. So the trestle. Our train moves through the cypress canopy at track level, water visible between the ties on both sides in wet season. The Interstate 55 corridor runs nearly parallel to us all the way to Chicago — the freeway and the railroad, the same corridor, the same route, each era's preferred technology of movement.

The Manchac Swamp marks something of a threshold. Behind us: New Orleans and its parishes, the deep alluvial delta, the city that has always been a port and a destination. Ahead: the higher ground of the Florida Parishes — the southeastern corner of Louisiana that never flooded with the Red River deposits, that was settled differently, that has its own personality.

The Florida Parishes were, briefly and peculiarly, actually part of Spanish West Florida even after the Louisiana Purchase. The United States acquired them in 1810 through a short-lived rebellion — the Republic of West Florida lasted seventy-four days — and added them to the new state. Tangipahoa Parish, which we're entering around mile forty-eight, sits in the heart of that old West Florida territory. It was settled by Scots-Irish farmers coming south from the Carolinas and Tennessee, not by the French Creole planters who defined the river parishes. Different people, different crops, different churches. Strawberries rather than cane; Baptist rather than Catholic.

The Illinois Central ran through this country and founded towns along its right-of-way. Ponchatoula, just ahead, was platted as a railroad town. Hammond, our stop, was named for a man who sold timber rights to the IC in 1818 — though the railroad itself arrived decades later, it was the railroad that made the town.

Ponchatoula, population around seventy-five hundred — this is strawberry country. The Ponchatoula Strawberry Festival draws tens of thousands each spring, and the parish ships strawberries to markets across the region. The town was incorporated in 1820, which puts its founding right at the moment the Santa Fe Trail was opening up to the west and the country was just beginning to understand the size of what it had purchased. Ponchatoula is a Choctaw word, meaning something like "hanging hair" — a reference, probably, to Spanish moss. We'll see the recurring pattern as we move north into Mississippi: Indigenous place names preserved in the geography long after the nations that gave them were displaced. The placenames are a kind of memory that the land holds even when the history books pass over it.

Around us as we come into Tangipahoa Parish: twenty-eight percent wetland, twenty-eight percent forest. The landscape is starting to lift. We are, almost imperceptibly, climbing out of the alluvial plain.

At roughly mile fifty, the bedrock geology beneath us shifts — from that broad Cenozoic category of older sedimentary rock to genuine Holocene alluvium: clay, sand, and gravel deposited in the last eleven thousand years, since the end of the last ice age. That is geologically instantaneous. The fossils found in this zone reflect it: Rangia cuneata, a brackish-water clam; Littoraria irrorata, the marsh periwinkle; Mytilopsis, a small mussel. All are creatures of the coastal interface, of brackish marshes and tidal flats. They lived here when sea level was slightly higher, or when the river was depositing differently. They're in the sediment beneath the strawberry fields.

Beyond mile sixty — just past Hammond — the geology shifts again to Pleistocene prairie terraces: older, higher, drier ground, laid down between two and a half million and eleven thousand years ago. Light gray to light brown clay and sandy clay, the geologic survey says. That older, firmer surface is what lets Hammond sit a full twenty feet above sea level — modest by most standards, but here, on this coastal plain, it's the high ground. It's why Hammond was the place the IC chose for a depot rather than the swampier lowlands south of it.

Hammond, Louisiana — population around twenty-one thousand, the largest city in Tangipahoa Parish. Out the left window you'll see Southeastern Louisiana University, established here because Hammond had the rail connection and the slightly higher ground. The campus opened in 1925, during the same decade that the Great Migration was accelerating northward through this very station.

The IC depot here was a separation point — literally. Jim Crow laws required segregated waiting rooms, segregated cars, segregated everything. Black passengers who boarded here for Chicago entered through one door and exited through another. They rode in the colored car, usually directly behind the locomotive, where the smoke and cinders were worst. The same train, the same tracks, the same northward journey — divided. What the Migration represented was, among other things, the decision to make that journey one-way. To not come back to the separate door. Hammond is forty-five miles from New Orleans and forty-five miles from Baton Rouge, almost exactly equidistant. For a century it was a market town for the Florida Parishes. For the IC, it was a stop. For the people who passed through its depot heading north, it was a threshold.

We're climbing now, though you'd never feel it — a few hundred feet over the next hundred miles, spread so evenly the grade is nearly unmeasurable. But the land is telling us. The cypress swamp has given way to mixed pine and hardwood. The soil is firmer, better drained. The Pleistocene prairie terraces are taking over from the Holocene alluvium. We're leaving the Mississippi Alluvial Plain — that vast, young, river-built province — and entering the Southern Coastal Plain: a broader, older, drier ecoregion that stretches east to the Carolinas and north into Tennessee. The transition happens around mile fifty, and by the time we reach mile sixty it's visible in the tree line, in the color of the soil visible along the cuts, in the way the farmhouses sit up on slightly higher ground.

The watershed divide is still fifty miles ahead — around mile one hundred and ten, we'll cross from the Mississippi watershed into the South Atlantic-Gulf watershed, from water that drains to the Mississippi delta into water that drains more directly to the Gulf through shorter rivers. That crossing is invisible from the window. But it's real, and it matters: we are, slowly, moving off the map that the great river drew.

The town ahead was once called Uncle Sam — a name that stuck from the antebellum era, when a local plantation went by that handle and everything around it took the name by association. Someone, somewhere in the 1880s, decided Uncle Sam needed a more dignified address and renamed it Independence. The Illinois Central was already threading through by then, and the railroad is the reason most of these small Louisiana towns exist in a line at all — they weren't settled in a cluster and then connected; they were platted along the right-of-way and grew outward from the depot.

We've been riding on the Prairie Terraces since we left the alluvial bottom — Pleistocene-age sediments, clay and silt and fine sand, laid down somewhere between two and a half million and twelve thousand years ago. The ground under the wheels isn't bedrock in any ancient sense; it's old flood debris, sorted and re-sorted by the ancestral Mississippi as it wandered. The river is miles to our west now, but it shaped every foot of this. Around mile seventy, the geology shifts — we'll move onto Cenozoic sedimentary rock, the broader era that runs from sixty-six million years ago to the present. It's still soft country, still low, still built from what water left behind.

Shiloh. The name appears on maps all across the South — there's a Shiloh here in Tangipahoa, and the famous battlefield is four hundred miles northeast in Tennessee. The name comes from Hebrew scripture, meaning "place of peace." The Tennessee Shiloh is anything but — April 1862, twenty-three thousand casualties in two days. Southern families named crossroads and communities after biblical places of refuge; the war then wrote over those names with different meanings entirely.

The Illinois Central built its main line through this corridor in the 1850s, reaching from Chicago south toward New Orleans in a nearly straight run. Straight was the point — the IC's engineers chose the route for its flatness, the unbroken coastal plain that let them lay track fast and keep grades shallow. What they built turned out to be something else entirely, something they didn't plan for: the primary corridor of the Great Migration.

From roughly 1910 to 1970, somewhere between six and seven million Black Americans left the rural South. A large fraction of them left Mississippi. And the train they took — the one whose right-of-way we're riding right now — was the Illinois Central. The City of New Orleans. The Panama Limited before it. You didn't need to know anyone in Chicago; you just needed a ticket north, and the train would carry you up this exact spine, through these parishes and counties, across the state line, through Memphis, across the Ohio River, into the industrial city.

The Blues went north on this train. Muddy Waters, Memphis Minnie, Big Bill Broonzey — born or raised in the Mississippi Delta, arrived in Chicago by Illinois Central. The music that became Chicago Blues became rock and roll. The train is still running the same line.

Day, Louisiana — a populated place, the maps say. Sometimes that's all there is: a cluster of structures that earned a name, a post office that closed, a crossroads that persists. The landscape here is wetland and forest in roughly equal measure — Tangipahoa Parish runs about twenty-eight percent wetland, twenty-eight percent forest. Between the trees, small farms; hay, mostly, and some soybeans.

Around us now, the forest is beginning to shade toward something different. We're approaching the edge of the Southern Coastal Plain ecoregion — the Gulf Coast Flatwoods — and just ahead, around mile seventy, we crossed into the Southeastern Plains. The distinction matters: the Coastal Plain is wetter, flatter, dominated by longleaf pine and bottomland hardwoods adapted to standing water and high humidity. The Southeastern Plains are still low, still humid, but the drainage is slightly better, the uplands a little higher, the forest composition shifting toward mixed pine-hardwood. The change is subtle from a train window — you won't see a line on the ground — but the soils underfoot are telling a different story, and the farmers know it.

Kentwood, 1893 — the year the Great Northern reached Puget Sound, when railroad companies were threading lines into every corner of the continent. This one, a small Louisiana town near the Mississippi line, got its start from the Illinois Central. Population held around two thousand for most of the twentieth century. Kentwood is best known now as the birthplace of Britney Spears, born here in 1981. The town she grew up in was already in the long, slow contraction that followed the collapse of the timber economy — the longleaf pine that once covered this country was largely cut by the 1920s, the mills closed, and the towns built around them had to find something else or shrink. Most shrank.

Here's the thing about the Great Migration that gets lost in the broad numbers: it wasn't a single event, it was millions of individual decisions made by individual people, most of them made on a kitchen table or a church porch on a Sunday afternoon. A letter arrived from a cousin who'd gone north the previous spring — he was working in the stockyards, he was sending money home, he said come. Or a sharecropper did the arithmetic on his cotton crop for the third year running and the numbers came out wrong again, owing more at the end of the season than at the beginning. Or a man looked at what had just happened to his neighbor and decided tonight was the night.

The Illinois Central ran two directions. Southbound, it carried goods and some passengers. Northbound, through the first decades of the twentieth century, it carried a population. The Chicago Defender — the Black newspaper that circulated through the South, sometimes passed hand to hand because it was dangerous to be seen with it — actively encouraged the movement, printed the train schedules, ran the addresses of rooming houses in Chicago's South Side. Buying a ticket north on the IC was, for many, the most consequential act of a life. We're riding that same track now, in the opposite direction.

We've crossed the state line. Louisiana behind us, Mississippi ahead — and the ground beneath us carries that weight. Osyka sits just over the line, a small town in Pike County, population under four hundred now. Its peak was earlier in the twentieth century, when it was a modest railroad depot town. Pike County is named for Zebulon Pike — the explorer who gave his name to Pike's Peak in Colorado, a man who mapped territories most Americans had never seen. The county was organized in 1815, the year after the end of the War of 1812, when the nation was still sorting out what it owned and what it could hold.

Mississippi, 1955. Emmett Till was fourteen years old when he was murdered in the Delta, his body thrown into the Tallahatchie River. The men who killed him were acquitted by an all-white jury in sixty-seven minutes. His mother insisted on an open casket. A hundred thousand people filed past. The photographs ran in Jet magazine. Rosa Parks said later she was thinking of Emmett Till when she refused to give up her seat in Montgomery that December. The Civil Rights Movement has many starting points; Till's murder in Mississippi is one of the most cited.

The train passes through this state carrying that history the way the silt carries minerals — invisibly, in everything. The Black Belt, the plantation counties, the sharecrop economy — it's all embedded in the landscape we're crossing. The poverty numbers for Pike County are stark: median household income around forty thousand dollars, poverty rate above thirty percent. The numbers look like the Delta because the history is continuous with the Delta. The cotton economy, the Jim Crow laws, the violence that enforced them, the Migration that partially emptied these counties — it all connects.

To our right, the low country of Pike County, Mississippi — wetland and water covering about a third of the land surface. The Bogue Chitto River runs through here, draining south toward Lake Pontchartrain in Louisiana. We're approaching a subtle but real watershed divide around mile one-ten: the drainage on this side of the line runs south, toward the Gulf. On the far side, it begins to tip north, into the South Atlantic-Gulf watershed. The land looks the same. The water knows the difference.

McComb was built by the railroad. In 1872 — the same era when railroad land grants were platting towns across the West, when the Iron Horse was the engine of American settlement — the Illinois Central extended its line into Mississippi and established a division point here. A division point is where the railroad maintains its shops, its roundhouse, where crews change and engines are serviced. Towns built around division points had a different economic character than ordinary depot towns: steady, industrial, organized around skilled labor. McComb grew into the largest city in Pike County, and it grew because the IC needed it.

Out the left window, McComb — twelve thousand people, the most substantial city we've passed since leaving the New Orleans metro. The Illinois Central shops employed a significant Black workforce by the early twentieth century, and McComb became a center of Civil Rights organizing. In 1961, Robert Moses of SNCC arrived here and began the first voting rights campaign in Mississippi. The response was violent — organizers were beaten, a church was bombed, a young man named Herbert Lee was shot and killed by a state legislator in broad daylight in front of witnesses. The witnesses refused to testify. McComb is on the Mississippi Blues Trail for its music, but its deeper history runs through every act of ordinary courage it took to stand in line at a courthouse and try to register to vote in 1961 Mississippi.

What Moses and SNCC began in McComb in 1961 was part of a long contest over who Mississippi belonged to. The Migration had been drawing people north for fifty years by then — the very railroad we're on, carrying families north by the trainload. Those who stayed, or couldn't leave, or chose to fight, built the Civil Rights Movement in the places the Migration had started from.

There is a kind of reciprocal history here: the Illinois Central was simultaneously the escape route and the organizational spine. Porters on the IC — members of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, the union A. Philip Randolph built — carried the Chicago Defender south on their runs, distributing it to contacts in towns like McComb, Osyka, Hammond. The train carried people north; the newspaper the train carried south helped organize those who remained. The corridor moved in both directions, always.

Norfield — an unincorporated community in Lincoln County, a name on a map and not much else visible from the window. Lincoln County begins here, and it's different in one striking way from what we've been crossing: sixty-seven percent forest cover. The wetland and water give way to trees. The timber industry that cleared the longleaf pine is long past, and the land has grown back — mostly loblolly and shortleaf pine now, second or third growth, nothing like the original forest but forest nonetheless.

Lincoln County was organized in 1870, during Reconstruction — a legislature trying to build institutions in the aftermath of a war, carving new counties out of older ones, naming this one after the president who'd been dead five years. The county seat is Brookhaven, just ahead of us. We'll get there in the next segment.

The geology has settled into Cenozoic sedimentary rock — the broad era that began sixty-six million years ago with the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs and continues to the present. These are soft rocks, young in geological terms, still being shaped by the rivers that cross them. Beneath the pine forest ahead of us, the earth is slowly tilting north. The watershed divide we crossed around mile one-ten means the water here drains differently — no longer toward the Gulf but toward the larger Mississippi watershed to the north. The land looks like the land we left an hour ago. The deep geometry of it has already changed.

The forest closes right in on both sides now — sixty-seven percent of Lincoln County is trees, mostly pine and mixed hardwood, with the rest wetland. That's not accident. This Cenozoic bedrock beneath us — sedimentary rock laid down sometime in the last sixty-six million years — is soft, loamy ground that holds water. The soil here drains slowly, pools easily. Farmers learned to work around it. The crop data tells the story: hay and vegetables and field peas, not cotton. The big cotton money was east and north of here, in the river-bottom counties.

The Illinois Central Railroad built this line through here in the 1850s, and what it did was connect the bottom of Mississippi to Chicago in one unbroken rail corridor. That connection meant everything. When Black Mississippians began leaving in earnest — the Great Migration, peaking after 1910 and again after 1940 — this was the track they rode. Not a metaphor: this specific right-of-way, this corridor we're rolling up right now. A family in Brookhaven or Hazlehurst could walk to a station, buy a ticket, and arrive in Chicago's South Side without changing trains. The Illinois Central's City of New Orleans ran this route for decades. Arlo Guthrie immortalized the train in song in 1971, but the migration that mattered was the human one — something like six million people across those decades, most of them riding lines exactly like this one, trading the sharecropper's ledger for the factory floor and the Blues clubs of the South Side. We are on the spine of that movement right now.

Brookhaven. County seat of Lincoln County, population around twelve thousand. The Illinois Central platted this town in 1858 — the railroad made it, gave it a name borrowed from Brookhaven, New York, and then essentially owned it for a generation. There's a harder history here too. In 1955, the same year Emmett Till was murdered in the Delta two hundred miles northwest of us, two Black voting-rights activists — Lamar Smith and George Lee — were killed in Mississippi. Smith was shot on the courthouse lawn in Brookhaven in broad daylight. No one was ever charged. That courthouse is two miles off our left window right now. The town has changed; that moment hasn't been forgotten.

Off to our right, three miles northeast, sits the Brookhaven-Lincoln County Airport — a small public-use field, paved runway, the kind of airport that dots the rural South. It's a thread worth noticing. Mississippi's inland counties built these strips during and after World War II, when the Army Air Corps trained pilots across the South's flat, clear-sky terrain. Many stayed on as municipal airports afterward. They're part of the same transportation layering we're riding through: the old Indian traces became military roads, the military roads became railroad routes, the railroad routes shaped which towns got airports, which towns got the highways. Motion begets motion. Infrastructure accumulates in the same corridors for centuries.

If you look right, you might catch a glimpse of the airport landmark — three nautical miles northeast of downtown Brookhaven. Small field, generally quiet. What's interesting isn't the airport itself but what it represents: by 2011 and 2015, when its most recent improvements were documented, rural Mississippi was still investing in this infrastructure, still betting that air access mattered for a county of thirty-five thousand people. That's a particular kind of faith in connection. In a county where one in five residents lives in poverty, the airport is also a statement about aspiration — that Brookhaven intends to stay part of a larger world.

Wesson sits ahead at the boundary of Lincoln and Copiah counties — a small town of under two thousand people, part of the Jackson metropolitan orbit now. Copiah County takes its name from a Choctaw word, one of dozens of place names on this route drawn from the languages of the people who lived here long before the railroad. Copiah: the Choctaw called it that. The county itself was organized in 1823, two years after the Choctaw ceded this land under the Treaty of Doak's Stand. That treaty was signed in 1820. By 1823, the county existed. By 1830, the Choctaw were removed entirely under the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek. The timeline is brutal in its speed.

Copiah County has a Reconstruction-era story worth sitting with. In 1875, Democratic rifle clubs in Mississippi ran a coordinated campaign of terror against Black voters and Republican officeholders — the so-called Mississippi Plan. Copiah County was one of the centers of it. The tactic worked: voter suppression through organized violence collapsed the Republican coalition that had briefly given Black Mississippians real political power. A decade later, in 1883, a Copiah County sheriff named John Print Matthews was murdered — shot — after he tried to protect Black voters. The New York Times covered it. Congress debated it. Nothing changed. The Mississippi Plan became a template that spread across the South, institutionalizing Jim Crow through violence and then through law. We're riding through ground where American democracy was, for several decades, deliberately dismantled and rebuilt as something else entirely.

Hazlehurst. This is a stop — if you're getting off, this is yours. But if you're riding through, look left at the station and think about Robert Johnson. The Delta Blues guitarist — the one the legend says sold his soul at a crossroads — was born in Hazlehurst in 1911. Or at least that's the most documented account; Johnson's origins were disputed even in his lifetime, and he spent time in the Delta further north. But Hazlehurst has the birth certificate. Johnson died in 1938 at twenty-seven, cause uncertain, in Greenwood, Mississippi. In his short life he recorded twenty-nine songs, almost none of them heard widely until the 1960s British Invasion when Keith Richards and Eric Clapton traced the roots of rock and roll back to this county, this man, this ground we're passing through.

Here at Hazlehurst, around milepost 150, we cross an invisible but real boundary — the watershed divide between the Lower Mississippi drainage and the broader South Atlantic-Gulf system we've been riding through. Water north of here drains toward the Mississippi River; water south of it drains toward the Gulf by other routes. Watersheds shape everything: which rivers were navigable, which routes the Choctaw and Chickasaw used, where the early settlers went, where the towns grew. The Illinois Central's engineers followed these drainages instinctively when they laid the route — it's the path of least resistance, quite literally. The train almost always is.

Something's happening beneath us that we should name before we miss it. Around milepost 180, the bedrock shifts — the Cenozoic sedimentary rock we've been riding over gives way to Late Eocene rock, 37.8 to 33.9 million years old. That's sandstone, clay, chalk, and limestone — harder, more structured, the kind of rock that was once seafloor. Because here's what the Late Eocene was: a warm, shallow tropical sea covered much of what is now the Gulf Coast states. Mississippi was underwater. The fossils prove it. In the rock just ahead of us, paleontologists have found Turritella mississippiensis — a marine snail, coiled tight, named for this state — and Solarium triliraium, another marine gastropod. Nucula sphenopsis, a tiny clam. These creatures lived in that shallow Eocene sea roughly 48 million years ago, died, settled into sediment, and became stone. We are about to ride over them. The land we call Mississippi was, for tens of millions of years, the bottom of an ocean.

Crystal Springs ahead — population just under five thousand, Copiah County. The name comes from the springs that once fed the town's water supply, now largely paved over. What the town is known for in the agricultural record is tomatoes. At its peak in the early twentieth century, Crystal Springs shipped more tomatoes than anywhere else in Mississippi — it called itself the "Tomato Capital of the World." That economy was built on sharecropper and tenant labor, overwhelmingly Black, working the same land under conditions barely distinguishable from what came before emancipation. The tomato boom faded after World War II, partly as mechanization changed what large-scale agriculture needed. Many of the hands who had worked those fields rode the Illinois Central north. They didn't go back.

We're entering Hinds County now — the most populous county in Mississippi, home to Jackson. The population shifts sharply: Lincoln and Copiah counties, back behind us, each had under thirty-five thousand people; Hinds County has two hundred twenty-six thousand, nearly a quarter million. The land cover shifts too: eighty percent developed, only twenty percent pasture. The rural pine forest and wetland we've been riding through starts to give way to suburban edge, strip development, the infrastructure of a mid-sized Southern city. Jackson is the state capital, and the Illinois Central has been pointing us toward it since we left the Louisiana border. We haven't arrived yet — but you'll notice the density of road crossings increasing, more vehicles at the grade crossings, more buildings close to the right-of-way. The city is beginning to announce itself.

A few miles ahead, off the tracks near Terry in Hinds County, stands the Dudley Jones House — built in 1907 in Queen Anne style, still standing, on the National Register of Historic Places. 1907 is a specific moment: Mississippi had been under its 1890 constitution for seventeen years, the one designed explicitly to disenfranchise Black voters through poll taxes and literacy tests. The Progressive Era was underway in northern cities. And in rural Hinds County, someone named Jones built a Victorian house. It's a small thing. But it's also a date — 1907 — when the legal architecture of Jim Crow was fully in place, the Great Migration was just beginning to accelerate, and life in a Mississippi county like this one was simultaneously ordinary and governed by extraordinary violence and exclusion. The house stood through all of it.

Right around here — milepost 180 — the bedrock shifts beneath us, and it's worth pausing on. We've been riding over undifferentiated Cenozoic sediment for the last sixty miles, geologically young stuff. Now we move onto Late Eocene rock: 37.8 to 33.9 million years old, sandstone and clay and chalk and limestone. This rock was seafloor. The Gulf of Mexico's ancestral waters covered Mississippi in the Eocene, a warm shallow sea teeming with the snails and clams whose fossils turn up in road cuts and creek banks all around here — Turritella mississippiensis, that coiled marine snail named for this very state. Then the sea retreated. The sediment compacted into stone. Rivers came, deposited loess and alluvium on top, and eventually the Illinois Central laid its tracks across the whole layered story. Every mile of this route is a page in that record. We're reading it in the wrong direction — riding over the last page first, working backward toward the oldest — but the book is complete.

Jackson. State capital, largest city in Mississippi, and for the men and women who rode this line north through the mid-twentieth century, it was the last major stop before the Delta opened up in earnest. The Illinois Central pulled out of here loaded — with workers, with families, with everything they owned packed into the colored cars. The station has seen a million departures. Some of those passengers were never coming back. A few were carrying the first verses of songs that would rename American music.

The rail corridor we're riding was not chosen arbitrarily. The Illinois Central found the path of least resistance through this terrain in the 1850s — which meant following the same gentle ridgelines and stream valleys the Natchez Trace had traced for a century before that, and before the Trace, the same routes the Choctaw and Chickasaw nations traveled for centuries more. Transportation routes in this country tend to be very old. The valley is the valley; the pass is the pass. We inherit the path.

Off to the left, that's Hawkins Field — Jackson's secondary airport, a joint civil-military field that dates in its current form to the Second World War era. General aviation now, mostly. It sits close-in to the city the way wartime airfields always do; they needed them near the industrial and population centers, near the rail lines. Notice how the transportation layers stack: the old Trace route, the railroad, the road grid, the airfield — all reading the same geography.

The ground beneath us right now is Late Eocene — roughly 37 to 34 million years old. Sandstone, clay, chalk, limestone, all laid down when a shallow sea covered this part of North America. We mentioned the Loess Plains earlier; that's the biome. But the bedrock underneath the loess tells an older story. Those fossil shells we noted — Nucula, Hilgardia, Calorhadia — marine bivalves, marine gastropods, creatures of a warm subtropical sea that no longer exists. The sea drained. The land rose slowly. Then the Mississippi system spent millions of years covering everything in silt from the interior of a continent. What we're riding over is layer upon layer of time, each readable if you know the script.

The community ahead is called Pocahontas — one of a handful of Mississippi placenames drawn from Native nations or figures. The Choctaw word for this river country, the Yazoo drainage, referred to the people of the river. French explorers transliterated those names onto the land, and the names outlasted the nations that gave them. The English-speaking settlers kept the names, sometimes corrupting them, sometimes preserving them nearly intact. That's a pattern we'll keep seeing as we push north.

Hinds County, which we're just leaving, has a poverty rate pushing 21 percent. Yazoo County ahead runs nearly 30. These numbers are not surprising to anyone who knows the history of the Black Belt — the arc of counties across the Deep South named first for soil color, then for the demographic legacy of the plantation economy. The cotton that made this land productive in the nineteenth century required enslaved labor on a massive scale, and after emancipation the sharecropping system that replaced slavery kept the same families bound to the same fields under different terms. The Illinois Central offered a way out. Between 1910 and 1970, roughly six million Black Americans left the South. A significant fraction of them left on this line.

Flora. Population under two thousand. It sits in Madison County, which is noticeably more prosperous than its neighbors — median household income nearly twice Yazoo County's. That's the Jackson metro influence pulling north along the corridor. Beyond Flora, the city's gravity fades, and we're back in agricultural Mississippi, soybean and cotton country. Notice how quickly the land cover shifts when you move ten miles off the interstate spine.

Here's a thing worth sitting with as we watch the fields slide by. The Illinois Central ran what was called, informally, the "Chicken Bone Special" — the name came from the fried chicken passengers brought aboard because the dining car didn't serve Black travelers with the same access it served white ones. Chicago-bound families would pack food for the whole journey. The train left New Orleans, came through Jackson, through the Delta towns ahead of us, up through Memphis, into Cairo, Illinois, and then into Chicago's Twelfth Street Station. Robert Abbott, the publisher of the Chicago Defender — the Black newspaper that actively recruited Southern readers to come north — ran train schedules and job listings side by side. The paper was smuggled into Mississippi by Pullman porters because distributing it openly was considered dangerous. Abbott understood that the train was the instrument of transformation.

Bentonia. Population just over three hundred. A town this size doesn't make it onto most maps, but it's on the Mississippi Blues Trail, and it should be. Bentonia is home to a distinctive regional blues style — the Bentonia school — darker, more minor-key, more modal than the Delta blues most people think of. Skip James recorded his essential work here in the 1930s. The style may trace to West African tonal patterns brought to this county with the enslaved population. It's one of those cases where the music carries a geography inside it — you can hear, if you listen carefully, that it came from this particular soil.

Somewhere around milepost 230, the geology beneath us will make a quiet transition — from the Late Eocene sedimentaries we've been riding for the last fifty miles into broader Cenozoic rock, geological shorthand for the last sixty-six million years. It's also near there that we'll officially enter the Mississippi Alluvial Plain — the Delta proper, the bottomlands built entirely by the river's millennial silt deposits. The ground will look the same to the eye. It won't be. The alluvial plain is among the most fertile agricultural land on earth, and it was that fertility that made the cotton economy here so extractive, so violent, so total. Every acre of Delta bottomland someone wanted required draining swamp, clearing timber, and — for most of the nineteenth century — human beings in bondage doing that work. The land looks flat and simple. It is neither.

Yazoo City. County seat, river town, named — twice removed — from the Yazoo nation by way of Robert de La Salle, who paddled past here in 1682 and called the river the Rivière des Yazous. La Salle's French gave way to English, the name survived, and the city that grew up here did so on the strength of cotton and the Yazoo River itself. The river bends close here. It was a steamboat stop before it was a rail stop. The Mississippi River steamboat era — running roughly the same decades as the early Illinois Central, 1811 into the early twentieth century — moved cotton south to New Orleans and goods north into the interior. When the rail came, it didn't kill the river trade immediately; for a generation both systems overlapped, competing and sometimes cooperating. Yazoo City sits at the seam of those two transportation eras.

We're now well into Yazoo County, population under thirty thousand, poverty rate near thirty percent, the land cover shifting toward cropland — forty percent, the data says, against only twenty percent forest. Cotton and soybeans, row after flat row. This is the agricultural Mississippi that most of the country doesn't see. The towns between here and the Delta proper are small: county seats hanging on, river landings that no longer have rivers calling, crossroads communities where the school consolidated and the grocery store closed and the young people left on this very rail line or on US 49. The median income here is $41,000. The national median is nearly double that. These numbers accumulate into a geography of consequence — a place the broader economy has not found a way to include.

Eden. A village; 133 people at the last count. The name is common across the American South — settlers naming new clearings after the paradise they hoped to build. The Edens rarely became what their names promised. This one is no different: a modest community at a crossroads, holding on. We'll pass it in a moment.

Ahead of us now, the Delta flattens further. The alluvial plain takes over the whole horizon. We are moving deeper into the heart of what James C. Cobb called "the most Southern place on earth" — and also into the place that gave American music more than any other geography its size. Blues, gospel, rock and roll: all of them trace ancestry to these fields and these small towns. The people who left — who rode this line north with their fried chicken and their Defenders and their determination — carried the music with them. Chicago would not have sounded the way it did without the Yazoo Delta. Neither would Memphis. The train goes on.

The fields out both windows — soybeans low and green, cotton stalks where last season's harvest was picked — are sitting on some of the youngest bedrock in the country. Cenozoic sediments, deposited over the last 66 million years by rivers not entirely unlike the one we've been shadowing. The soil here is so rich that a single acre can pull more than a bale of cotton, and that richness comes directly from the river's long habit of flooding, retreating, flooding again. Everything we're looking at was once river bottom.

The Illinois Central Railroad — the line we're riding — was completed through this stretch of Mississippi in 1855, thirteen years before the transcontinental railroad captured the country's imagination. The IC didn't connect coasts. It connected Chicago to the Gulf, and in doing so it stitched the cotton Delta to the industrial North with a single thread of iron rail. Farmers used it to ship bales north. Then, starting around 1910 and accelerating sharply after 1916, something else moved north on those trains. People. Black Mississippians, leaving the sharecropping system, the debt peonage, the legally enforced terror of Jim Crow, heading for Chicago, Detroit, St. Louis — industrial cities where the wage, however meager, was at least a wage. By the 1970s, six million people had made that journey. This track was one of their main corridors. We're riding the literal physical spine of the Great Migration.

A handful of buildings near the Yazoo River — Thornton, an unincorporated community that never quite became a town. U.S. 49E runs through it, paralleling us to the east. The Yazoo is close here, though you won't see it through the trees and the flat cropland. The river's name comes from the Yazoo people, one of the Natchez-confederated nations the French encountered and eventually nearly destroyed in the 1720s. That name has outlasted the people who gave it, the French who fought them, and the antebellum plantations that followed. The river keeps it alive, flooding these fields every decade or so, reminding everyone who is really in charge of the land.

There's a layering of routes in this part of Mississippi that takes a moment to see but, once seen, you can't unsee. Beneath us, the Illinois Central. Parallel to it to the east, U.S. Highway 49. Winding close by, the Yazoo River — which was the highway before any of those, the water road that Choctaw and Chickasaw traders paddled for centuries before cotton was king. And threading above us, occasionally, the approach corridors to the small general aviation airports scattered through the Delta — Greenwood has one, as do several smaller communities. Each layer of infrastructure was built by a different era's dominant logic. The river, by topography. The railroad, by the cotton economy's need to reach Chicago. The highway, by the automobile's twentieth-century democracy of motion. The airports, by New Deal and wartime federal investment. All of them running roughly the same direction, because geography left them no choice. The land is flat, the destination is north.

Tchula. Population around 1,650 today — it was 2,300 in 2000, and the trajectory is familiar across Holmes County. What's less familiar is what happened here in 1981: Eddie James Carthan, Tchula's first Black mayor, elected on a wave of post-Voting Rights Act civic energy, was convicted on a murder charge that most civil rights observers and the Congressional Black Caucus believed was fabricated by local white political opponents who wanted him removed from office. He served three years in prison. The convictions were eventually reversed. Tchula kept going, smaller each decade, but it kept going.

The name Tchula is Choctaw — one of several dozen Mississippi place-names that carry the Choctaw language forward even as the Choctaw Nation itself was dispossessed from this land. The 1830 Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, signed about forty miles east of here, ceded the last major Choctaw holdings in Mississippi to the United States. It was the first removal treaty under the Indian Removal Act. Chief Greenwood LeFlore — whose name you'll hear again in about twenty minutes when we reach Leflore County — was among the signatories, trading his nation's homeland for personal land grants and a Mississippi plantation of his own. He lived out his life in Mississippi, a Choctaw man on Choctaw soil, while most of his people walked west to Indian Territory. The placenames stayed. Everything else was taken.

Oswego is listed by the federal government as a populated place. In practice, it's a ghost town — one of several we're passing through this stretch of Holmes County, and worth naming as such. Ghost towns in Mississippi don't look like the ones in the Mojave, no collapsed saloons or sun-bleached wood. Here, the abandonment is subtler: a concrete foundation where a cotton gin stood, a chinaberry tree marking where a house was, a crossroads store long closed. The Delta's ghost towns didn't fail because the railroad bypassed them or the silver ran out. They emptied because the mechanization of cotton agriculture in the 1950s and 60s eliminated the sharecropper economy that had populated them, and those displaced sharecroppers — many of them — got on the Illinois Central and rode north.

Let me tell you about Emmett Till, because we're approaching the county where he died and this land deserves that accounting before we arrive.

Till was fourteen years old, from Chicago — South Side, the very endpoint of this railroad's migration corridor. In the summer of 1955 he came south to visit relatives near Money, Mississippi, a small community we'll pass in a few minutes. On August 24th he went into a store there. A twenty-one-year-old white woman named Carolyn Bryant — later Carolyn Bryant Donham — claimed he had grabbed her hand, whistled at her, and made a suggestive comment. Her husband Roy Bryant and his half-brother J.W. Milam drove to the relatives' house in the middle of the night, three days later, and took the boy. They beat him, shot him in the head, wired a 75-pound cotton gin fan around his neck, and dropped him in the Tallahatchie River.

Three days after that, a fisherman found his body.

Mamie Till, his mother, insisted on an open casket funeral in Chicago. She wanted the world to see what had been done to her son. Jet magazine published the photographs. The NAACP's membership rolls surged. The Montgomery bus boycott began four months later.

Bryant and Milam were acquitted by an all-white jury in sixty-seven minutes. Protected by double jeopardy, they told the full story to a Look magazine reporter for money, in 1956. Carolyn Bryant Donham told a biographer decades later that parts of her testimony were not true.

Emmett Till was fourteen. The cotton gin fan is still in the Tallahatchie River.

Sidon — a town that's been here since 1829, named for the ancient Phoenician city, in that habit nineteenth-century Mississippians had of giving their settlements the names of the Old World's great ports. The population is around 300 now, part of the Greenwood micropolitan area. It sits in Leflore County, named for the same Greenwood LeFlore who signed the Choctaw removal treaty. The county seat, Greenwood, was named for him too. The man's name is everywhere; his nation is not.

Leflore County is 80 percent cropland — that figure, from a bird's-eye view, is almost unimaginable. Nearly four out of every five acres, soybeans and cotton and corn, flat to the horizon. What made this possible geologically is what we've been calling alluvium and loess — the river-laid silt and the wind-blown dust that together built a soil horizon of almost absurd fertility. Loess — that fine, buff-colored, wind-borne silt — was carried here during the last ice age by prevailing winds off the glacial outwash plains to the north and west. It mantles the uplands, sometimes thirty feet deep. Mixed with the alluvial clays of the river bottoms, you get the Black Belt soils — dark, sticky, incredibly productive, and the ecological reason that cotton could be grown here at an industrial scale. The same soils that made this land valuable enough to enslave hundreds of thousands of people to work it. The geology is never innocent.

We're pulling into Greenwood — population around 12,000, county seat of Leflore County, and a city that carries about as dense a Civil Rights history as any in Mississippi. This is where Fannie Lou Hamer began her voter registration work in the early 1960s, where SNCC — the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee — established one of its key Delta offices, where federal officials were pressured to provide food aid to Black Mississippians who'd been cut off from federal surplus commodities as punishment for attempting to register to vote. The Cotton Street fire of 1963, which destroyed the SNCC office. The shooting of James Travis on the road just outside of town. This was the front line — not in a metaphorical sense, but literally: Greenwood was where the civil rights movement fought a specific, sustained battle for the right to vote in the most dangerous state in the country, in the years when that right could get you killed.

And underneath all of it: the cotton market. Greenwood was for decades the world's second-largest cotton market, after Memphis. The money that built these streets came from the same labor system the civil rights movement was tearing down.

Greenwood sits at the confluence of the Yalobusha and Tallahatchie rivers, which come together here to form the Yazoo. That confluence made it a significant river port before the railroad arrived — and then the Illinois Central made it a rail center, and the confluence mattered less. Transportation infrastructure has a way of doing that: each new mode doesn't erase the old geography so much as redistribute its value. The river crossings and confluences that made a town's fortune in 1840 become scenic overlooks by 1940. What persists is the town itself, built around a reason that no longer fully applies, holding on with what it has. Greenwood has cotton memory and civil rights memory and a music history — Robert Johnson is said to be buried somewhere in Leflore County, though three different grave sites claim the distinction. The Delta Blues were assembled from components that exist in tension: African musical traditions, Christian worship, the specific misery of the sharecropper system, and the particular sound of a guitar playing alone in a big flat space. Greenwood is near the center of that geography.

Money, Mississippi. About a hundred people live here now, down from four hundred when a cotton gin and mill operated in the early 1950s. It's on a railroad line — this railroad line, almost certainly — and on a bend in the Tallahatchie River. The Bryant's Grocery and Meat Market, the store where Emmett Till went on August 24, 1955, was here. The building still stands, or what's left of it — a ruin now, the roof long collapsed, the walls giving way. The Emmett Till Interpretive Center in Sumner, about twenty miles west, has been working to preserve what can be preserved and mark what can be marked. The Mississippi Delta National Heritage Area encompasses this ground. But the store is a ruin, and the river runs where it ran, and the cotton gin fan is still down there somewhere. We're passing the place where it began.

There's a particular arithmetic of the Great Migration that becomes visible out here. Holmes County, which we passed through an hour ago, has a poverty rate near 35 percent. Leflore County, around 32 percent. These are among the highest in the United States. And those numbers are, in part, the residue of the Migration itself — the people who left took energy and labor and ambition north, leaving behind those who couldn't go or wouldn't, and the communities they left thin. Chicago's South Side — Bronzeville, the Black Metropolis — was built in part from this county's outflow. The music that came north with those migrants became the electric blues, became rock and roll, became most of what you hear today. The Delta gave Chicago Robert Johnson and Muddy Waters and Howlin' Wolf and Little Walter. Chicago gave them amplifiers, urban audiences, and a recording industry. The trade was real, even when it was also flight.

We're about sixty miles into this segment, rolling north through some of the most freighted ground in American history. The elevation hasn't changed — still barely above sea level, still the river's flat gift of silt. What changes, slowly, over the next hundred miles, is the weight of that specific history. It lifts a little as we push north. The Delta doesn't end sharply — it fades. But it fades. Ahead, the land begins, almost imperceptibly, to firm up.

Off the left window — Minter City, more a crossroads than a town, straddling the line between Leflore and Tallahatchie counties. The name comes from a planting family, but what you're looking at is really the land itself: Delta alluvium so deep that you could drill a thousand feet down and still not hit bedrock. Everything here — the fields, the drainage ditches running ruler-straight, the dark soil that looks almost black in morning light — is river gift, laid down over millennia by the Mississippi and its tributaries. We're sitting on one of the youngest landscapes in North America, geologically speaking.

The Illinois Central rail corridor we're riding was not an accident of route selection. When the IC pushed south in the 1880s, it was threading the only high ground reliable enough for track — natural levees and sandy ridges left by old Mississippi channels. The same logic had governed movement through the Delta for ten thousand years before that: the Choctaw, and before them the Plaquemine culture, moved along these same elevated spines between the water. Then in the early twentieth century, that same corridor became something the railroad engineers never planned for — the physical wire along which Black Southerners would travel north by the hundreds of thousands. The Illinois Central's own advertising described Chicago as "the land of hope." The train we're on is, in a real sense, the successor to those passenger cars packed with families carrying everything they owned.

Glendora. Population 154 at last count. A tiny place, easy to miss — but you should know its name. In August 1955, a fourteen-year-old from Chicago named Emmett Till was abducted from his great-uncle's home not far from here. His body was pulled from the Tallahatchie River a few miles north. The men who killed him were acquitted by an all-white jury in Sumner, the county seat, in sixty-seven minutes. His mother, Mamie Till-Mobley, insisted on an open casket in Chicago so the world could see what had been done to her son. Two months later, Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a Montgomery bus. She said later she thought of Emmett Till. A hamlet beside a cotton field — and one of the pivot points of the twentieth century.

The Tallahatchie River is just to our east here — the word is Choctaw, meaning "rock of waters" — and it will stay close to our route for another twenty miles or so. In 1955, it was both crime scene and attempted burial ground. Bryant's Grocery, where the incident that preceded Till's murder occurred, stood a few miles east of here in Money, Mississippi. The store is a ruin now, deliberately left that way as a kind of witness. The Emmett Till Interpretive Center in Sumner has worked for years to mark these sites, and the tension between preservation and the desire of some to simply let it erode is itself a live argument about who gets to decide what a landscape remembers. The river doesn't adjudicate. It just keeps moving.

Mikoma — just a mark on the map, a cluster of structures in the low cropland. Nothing remarkable visible from the window except what the land itself says: that flat, almost hypnotic geometry of drained Delta fields, the rows aligned by GPS now but following drainage logic that goes back to the first levee districts of the 1880s. Cotton is still grown here, though soybeans have taken much of the acreage. The market moves; the land stays.

It's worth pausing on this soil, because it is genuinely extraordinary. The Black Belt — the dark, fertile swath of soils that arcs from Mississippi up through Alabama — has two meanings. One is ecological: these are among the most productive agricultural soils on earth, dark with organic matter, clay-rich, moisture-retaining. The other meaning came later: because this was the best cotton land, it was where enslavers concentrated their largest operations, and so it became, by the mid-nineteenth century, the area with the highest proportion of Black residents in the South — a demographic reality that persisted long after emancipation. The soil determined the crop. The crop determined the labor system. The labor system determined who lived here. And who lived here, and under what conditions, determined who eventually had reason to leave. Geology and migration, joined at the root.

Hiram — another populated place that barely registers at speed, a few structures absorbed into the field geometry. Tallahatchie County as a whole has lost more than a third of its population since 1970. The out-migration that started with the Great Migration never really stopped; it just changed character — from escape from violence and sharecropping to the slower drain of mechanization and agricultural consolidation. A cotton picker that took fifty field hands in 1940 takes one operator now.

The numbers from this period are worth holding in your head as we ride. Between 1910 and 1970, roughly six million Black Americans left the South for northern and western cities — Chicago alone received perhaps half a million. The Illinois Central, the line we're on, was called "the Main Line of Mid-America" by its own marketers. It was also called, by the people riding it, simply "the freedom train." Not metaphorically. There are letters preserved from the 1910s and 1920s — people writing back to cousins still in the Delta, describing Chicago wages, Chicago winters, Chicago schools. "We don't have to take off our hats to no man up here," one letter said. The train we're on hauled Pullman cars through here a hundred years ago, and in the segregated South, the Pullman porters — all Black, required to answer to the name "George" regardless of their own — were among the most organized labor in the country. The Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, founded by A. Philip Randolph in 1925, was one of the first major Black labor unions. They organized on the Illinois Central. Here. On this route.

Chancy, unincorporated, on Highway 321 south of Lambert. The highway and the railroad have been running roughly parallel through the Delta for a century now — the car route and the train route serving the same corridor, pulling traffic in the same direction. What changes is who can afford which.

Lambert — a real town by Delta standards, just over twelve hundred people. You'll see grain elevators, which have replaced the cotton gins as the landmark structures of the Delta skyline. Soybeans now ship in bulk where cotton once went in bales. The transition happened quickly after the 1970s as commodity markets shifted, and the landscape followed — a different crop, similar logic, same dependence on the rail corridor to move it north.

The early military airfields mentioned in the spine are worth a word here. During World War II, the flat terrain of the Mississippi Delta made it ideal for training fields — dozens of grass strips appeared across this region between 1941 and 1945. They don't show from the train, mostly absorbed back into farmland, but they're part of the same transportation logic: the Delta's flatness that makes the railroad straight makes the runway long. Movement infrastructure layers here, one atop another — the river, the levee road, the rail line, the airstrip, the highway. Each generation adds its own route on the same flat canvas.

We're pulling into Marks — the county seat of Quitman County, one of the smallest counties in Mississippi by population. The station opened in 2018, one of the newer stops on the City of New Orleans route. Marks has a particular place in American memory: in 1968, Martin Luther King Jr. came here while organizing the Poor People's Campaign, and what he witnessed — children, he was told, going to school with empty stomachs — moved him to tears. He was assassinated before the campaign's march on Washington. Quitman County's poverty rate today is still above thirty percent. We stop here two minutes, then keep north.

Somewhere between Marks and the next stop, we cross an invisible line — not a county line, but a geological one. The bedrock beneath the alluvium is about to change. For the entire journey since New Orleans, the rock under all this river sediment has been undifferentiated Cenozoic — the broad, 66-million-year category of "young stuff." But approaching milepost 360, the bedrock transitions to the Kosciusko Formation: Eocene rock, specifically from around 43 million years ago, part of what geologists call the Claiborne Group. Irregularly bedded sand, clay, and some quartzite. The Eocene was a warm interval — warmer than today, sea levels higher, the Gulf of Mexico's margin further inland than it is now. The sediments being laid down in this region 43 million years ago were coastal-to-shallow-marine: beach sands, tidal muds, the occasional silica-cemented quartzite bed where water chemistry was just right. We can't see any of this from the train — it's buried under twenty to a hundred feet of younger alluvium — but you're riding over the memory of a warm Eocene sea.

Sledge — population 368, Quitman County. Small enough that the loss of a single employer remakes the town. The fossils found in the Eocene sediments near this general stretch tell you what that ancient sea held: Euspira rectilabrum, a coiled predatory snail; Longoconcha, a small elongate bivalve; Napulus fragilis, another mollusk — all marine invertebrates from around 72 million years ago, Late Cretaceous, slightly older than the Eocene transition we just crossed. They turn up in road cuts, farm drainage ditches, anywhere the thin veneer of alluvium is breached. Farmers find them sometimes — mistaking them for modern shells, which is understandable. They look barely different from what washes up on Gulf beaches today. Seventy-two million years is a long time to stay the same shape.

The recurring thread of placenames derived from Native American language is audible through this whole corridor. Tallahatchie — Choctaw for rock of waters. Yazoo — possibly from a tribal name, possibly from a Choctaw word for death. Pontotoc, Noxubee, Yalobusha. Mississippi itself: Ojibwe via French, "great river." These names are the deepest layer of the palimpsest we're riding through — the stratum beneath the plantation names, the railroad stop names, the county names honoring generals and governors. Leflore County, behind us now, was named for Greenwood LeFlore, the Choctaw leader who signed the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek in 1830, ceding what remained of Choctaw land in Mississippi to the United States in exchange for land in Indian Territory. He then chose to stay — took American citizenship, became a planter himself, kept enslaved people on land that had been his nation's. History doesn't offer clean exits.

Crenshaw, straddling the Panola-Quitman county line. The town name is a family name, English, from the planting era. The land around it is still in the same basic geometry it's been in since the drainage districts of the 1880s cut their first ditches: flat, managed, drained. Out ahead, just past milepost 360, we cross into Tunica County — and with it a subtle but real change in the landscape's character. The forest cover increases, the wetlands grow thicker, the agricultural geometry loosens. The Mississippi River is closer to the west. We're moving toward the river's margin, where the land is still arguing with the water about who owns it.

Sixty miles since we started this segment, and the arc is becoming clearer. We've moved through three counties, each one named for a different chapter of the same violent dispossession — Leflore for the Choctaw chief who signed away his nation's land, Tallahatchie for the river that tried to hide a murdered boy, Quitman for a governor who later fought for the Confederacy. The Illinois Central corridor knits them together, running straight north on the old natural levee spines, carrying soybeans now where it once carried cotton and people with everything packed into a single bag. Ahead: Tunica County, and the bedrock shift to Eocene sand and clay, and the land beginning its slow turn toward Memphis. We've got good miles still ahead of us.

The ground under us right now is Eocene sand and clay — the Kosciusko formation, laid down roughly forty-two million years ago in the shallow seas that covered this land long before the Mississippi River existed in anything like its current form. The river came later and remade everything, leaving behind the flat, black bottomland that we're crossing now. Thirty-three percent forest, thirty-three percent wetland — this is a county that is mostly still water and wood, even after a century and a half of cotton. The soil's dark fertility and the poverty that coexists with it are both written in those river sediments.

Tunica County has one of the highest poverty rates in Mississippi — thirty-one percent — and median household income that runs about half the national figure. That fact has been true in one form or another since Reconstruction. The county was named for the Tunica people, a confederacy of Indigenous nations who controlled this stretch of the lower Mississippi for centuries before European contact. Most of the Tunica eventually moved to central Louisiana during the colonial period, pushed by the same pressures — French alliance-making, Chickasaw raids, disrupted trade routes — that were fracturing every Native polity in the mid-South. The cotton economy that replaced their world arrived fast and left deep. By the 1840s, Tunica County was one of the wealthiest places in the United States, measured by the value of enslaved people and the acres planted in cotton. By 1900, most of that wealth had concentrated in Memphis banks. By 1950, the people who had worked the fields for nothing, then for near-nothing, began leaving. They left on trains very much like this one, heading exactly the direction we're going: north.

Savage is ahead of us — a crossroads community in Tate County, sitting where Mississippi Highways 3 and 4 meet. The name has no dramatic origin on record, but out here, along this corridor, even the unnamed places carry weight. Highway 3 runs almost due north-south through the Delta, paralleling the Illinois Central line, and it was one of the two or three roads a sharecropper family might walk to reach the nearest station, suitcase in hand, in the 1920s or 1940s. The geography of the Great Migration is always this specific: a particular road, a particular mileage, a particular train.

Emmett Till was fourteen years old when he was murdered in August 1955, about fifty miles southeast of where we are right now, in the town of Money, Mississippi. His killers were acquitted by an all-white jury in sixty-seven minutes — one juror later said they'd taken a soda break to stretch it out. Till's body was shipped home to Chicago in a casket, on a train. His mother, Mamie Till-Mobley, insisted on an open casket. Jet Magazine published the photographs. The resulting shock accelerated what historians now treat as the beginning of the modern Civil Rights Movement. Rosa Parks later said she thought of Emmett Till when she refused to give up her seat. The fields we're rolling through were the world that produced that crime — not as background, but as cause. The Delta plantation system, the sharecropping contracts, the county courthouses that administered white supremacy as ordinary law — all of it is right here, in the cotton and the flatness and the quiet.

Off to our left, near Mississippi Highway 3, sits Prichard — an unincorporated community between the old cotton towns of North Tunica and Arkabutla. The bedrock under us is shifting here from the Kosciusko formation into broader Cenozoic sedimentary rock — a sixty-six-million-year sweep of river-deposited material that records every sea-level change, every flood pulse, every geologic season since the age of dinosaurs ended. None of it is visible from the window; it's all buried under a few feet of alluvium. The land tells its geology only through the plants it grows and the water it holds.

Loess — wind-blown silt deposited during the ice ages, when glacial outwash plains to the north and west were exposed and dry — is what built the bluffs that will appear as we approach Memphis. The Mississippi Valley Loess Plains ecoregion that we're entering around milepost four hundred is one of the more geologically distinctive regions in North America: a narrow band of deeply loess-mantled uplands running along the eastern edge of the Mississippi floodplain from Illinois to Louisiana. The loess here is sometimes forty or fifty feet thick. It's extremely fertile, highly erodible, and it stands in vertical faces when it's cut — a property that allowed the Confederate defenders at Vicksburg to tunnel into it and live underground during the siege of 1863. The same silt that makes the soil rich makes the bluffs. The same bluffs that sheltered Confederate troops now anchor the eastern edge of Memphis.

Banks is a small populated place ahead in Tunica County — one of dozens of rural communities along this corridor whose economies turned entirely on cotton and then, when cotton mechanized in the 1940s and 1950s, had nothing left to turn on. The mechanical cotton picker, commercially introduced in 1944, eliminated the need for most field labor within about a decade. That single machine accelerated the Great Migration more than any other technological event. The people who had worked these fields by hand left. The towns that had served them shrank.

The Illinois Central Railroad — this line — was called "the Main Line of Mid-America." But among the Black communities of the Delta, it was called something simpler: the way out. The IC ran from New Orleans through Jackson, Memphis, and on to Chicago. A ticket cost money most sharecroppers didn't have, but the Illinois Central also recruited labor, and some migrants rode north on freight, or pooled money for a one-way coach seat. Between 1910 and 1970, approximately six million Black Americans left the South. About a third of a million came through Memphis. Most of the rest came through on roads and rails that converged on the same northern cities — Chicago, Detroit, Cleveland, St. Louis. We're riding the same corridor. The seats are different. The destination is the same.

We've crossed into DeSoto County now — population nearly two hundred thousand, median income roughly double what it is back in Tunica. DeSoto County is part of the Memphis metropolitan area, and you can feel it: the land is more developed, the towns are closer together, the infrastructure thickens. Marienette is a small community ahead of us. DeSoto County is the second-most populous county in Mississippi, largely because Memphis's suburbs sprawl south across the state line. The railroad corridor we're on was one reason this edge of Mississippi urbanized; the interstate infrastructure that paralleled it was another. The geography of movement shapes who lives where.

The old Yazoo and Mississippi Valley Railroad — a subsidiary of the Illinois Central — ran through this part of DeSoto County, and the towns along it developed in the rhythm that railroad towns always did: platted at regular intervals, sized by how far a farmer could haul a cotton bale to the gin by wagon in a day. That rhythm is roughly five to ten miles between towns, and if you look at the map of this corridor, you can still read it. The automobile eventually broke the rhythm — allowed farms to spread further, made the towns redundant — but the railroad fixed the initial spacing. Memphis itself was a railroad city before it was anything else: founded on the river, yes, but the IC and the Louisville and Nashville and the Southern Railway made it the largest inland cotton market in the world by 1900.

Lake View sits just south of Memphis, near the Mississippi-Tennessee line — on what the notes describe as the "former Yazoo and Mississippi Valley" right-of-way. We're almost out of Mississippi. The border is less than two miles ahead. The Yazoo and Mississippi Valley line was absorbed by the Illinois Central in 1882, which is to say that the same corporate entity that later carried the Great Migration north also built the infrastructure that locked Delta Black communities into the plantation system during Reconstruction. Railroads in the postbellum South were instruments of both control and escape, depending entirely on who was buying the ticket and where.

We cross into Tennessee — into Shelby County — and the character of the land outside changes within a few miles. The wetland and row-crop flatness gives way to a more mixed landscape, forty percent forest, forty percent developed, and the skyline of Memphis begins to assemble itself to the southeast. Memphis is the first major city on this entire leg. It sits on the Chickasaw Bluffs — those loess bluffs we mentioned earlier — above the east bank of the Mississippi. The Chickasaw called these bluffs home for centuries; Hernando de Soto's expedition reached the river somewhere near here in 1541. The city of Memphis was incorporated in 1826, named after the ancient Egyptian capital on the Nile, which its founders evidently considered an appropriately grand comparison for a city on a great river.

By the Civil War, Memphis was the sixth-largest city in the Confederacy and the single most important inland cotton market in the South. The Union captured it in June 1862 in a river battle that lasted about ninety minutes. After the war, Memphis became a destination for freed people, for labor, for the convergence of African American musical traditions that were already in motion up and down the Delta. By the 1920s, Beale Street was one of the most famous Black commercial districts in the country — a place where W.C. Handy had lived and written, where the blues formalized into something the rest of the world could hear.
