Ahead in Memphis: Electraphonic Recording, a studio and label that continues the city's deep tradition of recorded sound. Memphis is where the Blues Trail, which we've been tracking implicitly since Jackson, reaches its northern terminus in the Delta tradition — and simultaneously where that tradition transforms. Sun Studio, Stax Records, Hi Records — they're all within a few miles of us. Elvis Presley recorded "That's All Right" at Sun in July 1954. Otis Redding recorded "(Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay" at Stax in 1967, three months before he died in a plane crash. Isaac Hayes recorded "Shaft" here in 1971. The thread running through all of it is the specific sound of the Delta — the blues — carried north and electrified and transformed into something new. Every one of those records carries the sediment of this land in it, the weight of the migration, the particular grief and exuberance of people who left one world and made another.

North of Memphis, the bedrock under us shifts to Late Eocene sedimentary rock — sandstone, clay, chalk, and limestone laid down between thirty-eight and thirty-four million years ago, when a warm, shallow sea covered this part of North America. Above that is recent alluvium, the Mississippi River's gift: loam, sand, gravel, clay, all of it deposited and redeposited across millennia of flooding. The Loosahatchie River — a tributary of the Mississippi — runs roughly parallel to us now, draining the flat terrain north of the city. The name is Chickasaw. Most of the river names in this part of Tennessee and Mississippi are Chickasaw, or corruptions of Chickasaw, which is a reminder that the geography was already fully named before European maps existed.

Ahead near the Loosahatchie River sits the Memphis International Raceway — now Darana Motorsports Park — an oval track that has hosted ARCA and American Speed Association events, tucked between the river bottoms and the northern suburbs. Auto racing arrived in this corridor in the same period that the Interstate highway system was being built through it, and the two are related: the postwar American faith in speed and pavement expressed itself in racetracks as surely as it expressed itself in interstates. The Illinois Central line we're riding was the corridor before the interstates. The interstates were the corridor before the airlines. Each layer of American transportation infrastructure got laid on top of the previous one, and you can see all of them from this window — rail, road, airfield — stacked in the same flat bottomland, all of them tracing the same ancient path between the river and the bluffs.

The soil shifts here — look at the cut banks anywhere you can see them. We're on loess, the wind-blown silt the glaciers ground up and the Mississippi's floods laid down over centuries. It's a strange material: stands in near-vertical walls, drains poorly, stains orange-red in the sun. Farmers here grow soybeans and cotton in it, the same rotation that's been turning over since before the Civil War. The land is mostly forested now — second-growth hardwood — but the fields appear in intervals, reminding you what this county was made for. Shelby County behind us is the most populous in Tennessee. Tipton ahead is its quieter neighbor, cotton country still.

units.text: The Late Eocene rock beneath us — sandstone, chalk, limestone — is roughly 35 to 38 million years old, laid down when a shallow sea covered this part of the continent. We mentioned it briefly coming into Memphis; here we're still riding over it, though the surface reads nothing like a seafloor. The loess cap is young, geologically speaking — a few tens of thousands of years — and it buries the older story. But the Eocene connection is the real one: a whale swam in that ancient sea. Basilosaurus cetoides, an early whale, 50 to 60 feet long, breathed air and hunted fish over the very rock that underlies our tracks. It's a creature that bridges worlds — descended from land mammals that returned to the sea — and its fossils turn up in the chalk and marl of this formation across the Mid-South. The chalk is the giveaway: chalk means marine, means open water, means a world completely unlike the cotton rows and soybean flats out the window.

Tipton community — now absorbed into the town of Atoka — comes up briefly on our left. Its own ZIP code, 38071, is the ghost of a more distinct identity. This is common out here: the railroad platted or anchored dozens of these small nodes, and over time the highway and the consolidation of rural services quietly dissolved them back into whichever town had the courthouse and the stoplight. The post office holds the name, even when the community itself has faded into subdivision and county road.

We've been on the Illinois Central corridor since Memphis — or rather, the route the City of New Orleans follows, which is the old Illinois Central line running roughly north from New Orleans through Jackson, Memphis, and all the way to Chicago. It is one of the most freighted routes in American social history. From the 1910s through the 1970s, somewhere between four and six million Black Southerners left the rural South for Northern cities — Chicago above all — and a very large share of them rode this railroad, or drove the highway that shadowed it, or followed the exact track of towns it served.

The Illinois Central didn't set out to carry a social revolution. It set out to carry cotton and timber south to New Orleans and manufactured goods north. But it ran a Chicago Defender route — the Black newspaper distributed along the line, smuggled in packages by Pullman porters — and the Defender ran ads, job listings, letters from relatives who'd made it north. It was a physical information network. A family in Lauderdale County — where we're headed — could read, in their own language, what wages looked like in the stockyards, what it felt like to walk a street where no one told you which side to stay on. The railroad carried the message and then, when enough families had read it, it carried the families.

Brighton — population just under three thousand. A small Tipton County town that sits in the Memphis Metropolitan Statistical Area, connected to the larger city's economic gravity even if it reads as thoroughly rural. The land around it is forest and field in roughly equal measure. These small nodes — Tipton, Brighton, Atoka — are the granular texture of a county that sends people toward Memphis or north; they're origin points on the Migration's spine.

Tipton County, which we're crossing now, was founded in 1823. By the 1850s it was Deep South cotton economy: enslaved labor, large plantations, the same world that ran from the Mississippi Delta up into western Tennessee. The county seat is Covington, just to our east, and it sits inside the geography of the antebellum Black Belt — the band of counties across the South where the soil and the slave economy locked together.

What that meant in practice, in terms of daily violence and enforced immobility, shaped everything that came after — including the Great Migration. People did not leave the rural South because things were merely uncomfortable. They left because of the threat of violence that was systematic and largely unpunished, because of sharecrop debt that was designed to be unpayable, because of the complete exclusion from political life. The Illinois Central was not an escape hatch so much as the first infrastructure that made leaving physically possible on a mass scale. Before the railroad, the geography itself enforced staying.

Just ahead, if you look east toward Covington, you're near the Canaan Baptist Church — we can't see it from the tracks, but it's worth knowing we're passing it. Congregation founded in 1868, three years after the Civil War ended. The building itself went up in 1916, now on the National Register of Historic Places. 1868 is the essential date: a congregation of formerly enslaved and newly freed people founding a church. It is the kind of institution that the Black community built first and fastest after emancipation, because the church was the one institution entirely their own — no white trustee, no landlord's permission, no planter's oversight. Canaan means promised land. That name was not casual.

Around milepost 450 the geology shifts under us, though you'd never know it from the window. We cross from the Late Eocene sedimentary bedrock — that ancient seafloor chalk and sandstone — onto Quaternary alluvial deposits. The changeover is the Mississippi River's doing. We're approaching the floodplain, and here the river has left hundreds of feet of sand, silt, clay, and gravel over the older rock. The alluvium is young in deep-time terms — the last two and a half million years, down to yesterday's flood pulse — and it's the geological canvas on which the entire cotton economy was written.

Fine alluvium is extraordinarily fertile. It is the reason the Mississippi Delta became the American cotton heartland, the reason this thin strip of western Tennessee counties was planted out to cotton before the Civil War and kept at it long after. The same river that made the soil capable also made it flood. And the effort to control that flooding — levees, drainage districts, channelization — is itself a story about who had the political power to get the Army Corps of Engineers to reroute a river for their fields.

Durhamville, on the right — a rural community in Lauderdale County, the second oldest town in the county. Founded by Colonel Thomas Durham around 1829 or 1830. He ran a store here. That was the unit of early rural commerce: a store at a crossroads, a man with a name that stuck to the place. The town predates the railroad by decades, which means it was already old when the tracks came through. Some of those early towns absorbed the railroad and grew; others like Durhamville held their shape and stayed rural.

We've crossed into Lauderdale County — its western border runs along the Mississippi River itself, about thirty miles to our left. Lauderdale County has been cotton country since the antebellum period, and unlike the counties north of Memphis, it never fully diversified. Two-thirds cropland by land cover today, with soybeans and cotton still dominant. Population about twenty-five thousand, median income roughly forty-six thousand — one of the lower figures we've seen this leg. The county seat is Ripley, east of us. Out the left window now, the land opens into the broad alluvial flat.

Lauderdale County sits inside the geography of the Emmett Till Memorial corridor. Till was murdered in August 1955 in the Mississippi Delta — across the river, in Tallahatchie County, Mississippi — but the world in which that murder happened, and the world in which it was followed by an all-white jury acquittal in sixty-seven minutes, extended north through counties exactly like this one. Western Tennessee and the Delta were economically and socially continuous: the same sharecrop system, the same white supremacist political order, the same terror used to control Black labor and movement.

The Till murder became the first event of the Civil Rights era to achieve genuine national and international attention, in part because Till's mother, Mamie, insisted on an open casket in Chicago. She wanted the world to see what Mississippi had done to her son. That choice — to make visible what the South had always kept local, local, local — cracked something open. Rosa Parks later said she was thinking of Emmett Till when she refused to move to the back of the bus in December of that same year, 1955.

The Illinois Central carried Till north to Chicago as a child. It carried his body back south for burial, and then it carried the grief and the outrage back north. The train didn't just transport people. It transported the story.

Gates — a small town in Lauderdale County, population around 660. It's listed as a majority-minority community, which in this context means what it always means out here: the demographics of slavery and sharecropping persisted in the land even as the formal legal structures changed. The Migration changed this, slowly. Every decade from 1910 through 1970, more people left than arrived. Gates kept its name and its place on the map, but not its population. The county lost people steadily to Chicago, to Memphis, to anywhere the Illinois Central went.

The mastodon is worth a moment before we leave this stretch. Mammut americanum — the American mastodon — lived in this region up to about 10,000 years ago, browsing the spruce forests that covered the mid-continent during the last ice age. Its fossils have been found in this same Quaternary alluvial system we're riding over. The mastodon was here when the first humans crossed this land — the people whose descendants gave the Mississippi River its name, an Ojibwe word, Misi-ziibi, the Great River. Those are the original placenames the leg spine calls out: the deep grid of Native American geography that the European settlers overlaid but never fully erased.

The mastodon, the alluvium, the ancient sea beneath — three timescales telescoping inside sixty miles of window. The cotton rows and the soybean fields are the newest layer, and they're already changing: the acreage planted to cotton has been declining for decades as commodity prices shift and irrigation costs rise. What this land looks like in another generation is genuinely open.

Fowlkes coming up ahead, just over the Dyer County line. Another small community, another post office anchoring a rural cluster. The geology has swung back briefly to Late Eocene bedrock around mile 460 and will stay variable as we move north. But the surface — that thick alluvial cap, the broad flat floodplain drainage — reads consistently from here to the Kentucky state line. We're in the heart of the Mississippi embayment, the trough the river has built and filled over millions of years. The land is saying one thing: this is the river's country, shaped by the river's patience.

The soil under those soybean fields — we've been crossing it for a while now, but it's worth a moment. This is Late Eocene sediment, deposited when a shallow sea covered this part of North America roughly 35 to 38 million years ago. Sandstone, clay, chalk, and limestone laid down in layers, then buried, then exposed again by erosion and the slow work of rivers. The crops don't care about the geology, of course — but the flatness does. That sea-bottom levelness is why farming here is so efficient, and so relentless.

This stretch of western Tennessee sits squarely on what historians call the Black Belt — not the soil type here, but the cultural and demographic region that stretches from Mississippi north and east, named for the density of Black population that the plantation economy produced and that the Great Migration began to drain. The Illinois Central Railroad, the line we're riding, was the physical channel of that migration. From the 1910s through the 1970s, hundreds of thousands of people stepped onto trains very much like this one in stations across Mississippi and Tennessee, bound for Chicago. They carried photographs, they carried church directories with names of cousins already north, they carried the knowledge that a train ticket cost less than a month's wages and that Chicago was sixteen hours away. Ida B. Wells had made the trip. Robert Abbott, founder of the Chicago Defender, had made the trip and then spent decades using his newspaper to urge others to follow. The Defender was smuggled south on the very mail cars behind the engine — Pullman porters passed copies hand to hand — because several Mississippi counties banned its distribution. The train we're on was the Underground Railroad of the twentieth century. Slower. Legal. No less desperate.

Newbern on the left — a quiet Dyer County town, founded 1857, on the eve of the war that would end the labor system that built this whole region. The railroad arrived first; the town grew around the depot. That sequence — rail line plotted, then town platted beside it — repeated itself hundreds of times across the South and West in the second half of the nineteenth century. The railroad makes the town. Sometimes the railroad also unmakes it, when a line is rerouted or a depot closes. Newbern held on. Population just over three thousand today.

Around milepost 500 we cross a quiet but significant boundary underfoot. The Late Eocene bedrock we've been riding over gives way to Quaternary alluvial deposits — material geologically young enough to include sediments laid down in our own era, the last two and a half million years. Quaternary is the geologic period we live in right now, encompassing the Ice Ages and everything after. The alluvium here — sand, silt, clay, and gravel — is flood-plain material from the Mississippi River system, in places more than a hundred feet thick. The river built this land by flooding it, abandoning it, flooding it again. Everything we're crossing is the river's slow autobiography.
Trimble just ahead — a small crossroads town straddling the Dyer-Obion county line, incorporated 1905. Fewer than six hundred people. Soybeans to the horizon.

Obion County now — a hundred percent cropland in the land-cover data, which is a remarkable number. The county was formed in 1823 and named for the Obion River, one of the lesser tributaries of the Mississippi system draining western Tennessee. The name is likely Chickasaw in origin, one of the dozens of Native American place names woven into the Mississippi Valley landscape — the recurring thread of Indigenous geography that outlasted the nations themselves. Chickasaw people controlled this territory for centuries before Andrew Jackson's Indian Removal Act of 1830 forced their expulsion west. The county was organized in 1824, six years before the Removal Act, while the Chickasaw were still present on this land.

Around milepost 510, notice the soil texture if you can see disturbed ground near the tracks. This is loess country — wind-deposited silt, blown off glacial outwash plains to the northwest during the Ice Ages and piled here in layers that can reach a hundred feet thick along the Mississippi bluffs, thinning eastward. Loess is extraordinarily fertile and extraordinarily unstable on slopes. It holds a vertical face almost like concrete when dry, then collapses catastrophically when wet. The bluffs along the Mississippi River in this region are loess bluffs — they look solid and geological but they're made of windblown dust. The same dust, reconstituted as topsoil, is part of why this county is a hundred percent in crops.

Union City on the left — county seat of Obion County, eleven thousand people, the largest town we'll pass between Newbern and the Kentucky line. Founded 1867, two years after the end of the Civil War, in the gap where the old agricultural order was collapsing and the new one — sharecropping, the crop lien system, debt peonage under a different name — was being constructed in its place. The name "Union City" in the postwar South is pointed. Tennessee had been bitterly divided; Obion County voted against secession in 1861. The town's founding in 1867 carries the politics of Reconstruction in its name.

The Illinois Central passed through here, and that mattered. The Blues traveled this corridor too — not just the people but the music. The Mississippi Blues Trail extends north through these Tennessee towns, tracking the movement of a musical form that grew from the Delta and migrated with the people who made it.

In 1955, a fourteen-year-old boy named Emmett Till was murdered in the Mississippi Delta, two hundred miles south of where we are. His murder and the acquittal of his killers became one of the catalysts of the Civil Rights Movement. But the geography matters: Till had come down from Chicago on the Illinois Central, visiting family in the Delta. He traveled this line, or its southern extension, in both directions. The train was the connection between the Chicago his family had built a life in and the Mississippi Delta his great-grandparents had never been allowed to leave.

That violence, that terror, that legal impunity — it was both what drove the Great Migration and what the migrants carried with them in memory, even after they arrived in Chicago. The train didn't erase the haunting. It transported it north, where it transformed into gospel, then blues, then jazz, then rhythm and blues, then rock and roll, then soul. Every musical genre that defines American popular culture in the twentieth century has its roots in what happened on this ground, in these flat fields, in the labor and suffering and creativity of people who had no choice about being here and then, when they finally had the choice, left on this train.

We've crossed into Kentucky — the state line is just behind us, almost imperceptible in this flat landscape. And on the right: Fulton, Kentucky. Population twenty-three hundred, shrinking. But Fulton once held one of the more improbable distinctions in American commerce: the Banana Capital of the World.

Seventy percent of all bananas imported into the United States passed through Fulton, because this was where the Illinois Central had its major refrigeration facilities. Bananas came by ship to New Orleans, then by train up the line — and here, in this small Kentucky town, the refrigerated cars were iced and the fruit was sorted before distribution north. At its peak, Fulton processed millions of bunches a year. The Illinois Central's icing facility employed hundreds. When refrigerated trucking made rail distribution obsolete in the mid-twentieth century, Fulton's economy went with it. The population in 1950 was over eight thousand. It's under twenty-four hundred now.

Water Valley just to the right — a tiny place, incorporated 1884, charter dissolved by court order in 2016. Two hundred and thirty-five people. The kind of town that appeared beside a railroad line, served a purpose, and then watched that purpose diminish. Kentucky has dozens of them along the Mississippi corridor.

Fulton County, Kentucky — named for Robert Fulton, inventor of the commercially viable steamboat, which is fitting because the Mississippi River forms the county's entire western boundary. The river is a few miles to our left now, invisible behind the bluffs and the floodplain timber, but its presence defines everything about this land. The bedrock here has shifted again — we're into Tertiary continental deposits, a mix of fine alluvium, gravel, and sand, undifferentiated, the catch-all category geologists use for the complex interfingering of river-deposited material west of the Tennessee River. Loess is in there too. The whole substrate is the river, sorted and re-sorted over millions of years.

Fulton County is the westernmost county in Kentucky, and by income data, among its poorest — median household income around $35,000, poverty rate over 27 percent. Hickman, the county seat, sits on a loess bluff above the Mississippi, a town that has been watching the river for nearly two centuries. The river does not watch back. It flooded Hickman repeatedly through the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, each time resetting the town's ambitions.

We're at the edge of Hickman County now — least densely populated county in Kentucky, a dry county, just over forty-five hundred people across a landscape that is mostly soybean field and bottomland timber. The county was formed in 1821, the same year the Santa Fe Trail opened for trade two thousand miles to the west, when this whole region was still Chickasaw territory, still contested, still being mapped by a young republic that had no clear idea what it had acquired from the French twenty years earlier.

The train continues north. The river keeps pace to our left, invisible but insistent. In a few miles the watershed beneath us will shift — we'll cross from the Mississippi drainage into the Ohio drainage, a continental divide so flat you could miss it if you blinked. But the river we've been following since New Orleans, the one that shaped this land down to its molecules, will finally let us go.

Off to the right, the land flattens into one of the emptiest counties in Kentucky — Hickman County, formed in 1821, the same year the Santa Fe Trail opened and a continent away, overland commerce was rewriting the map. Here, commerce moved by river. Fewer than forty-five hundred people in the whole county now, spread across fields of soybeans and corn on soil that the Mississippi built grain by grain. That silt underfoot is Tertiary — deposited anywhere from a million to sixty-six million years ago, long after the dinosaurs, in an age when this whole region was draining toward a sea that no longer exists. The loess came later, blown off glacial outwash plains during the Pleistocene ice ages. Good farmland, terrible for density. Hickman County is still a dry county — not a drop of legal liquor sold.

This corner of western Kentucky sits at the very end of the Great Migration's southern axis — the Illinois Central line we're riding was the iron spine along which hundreds of thousands of Black Southerners moved north between 1910 and 1970, trading the cotton fields and the violence of the Deep South for the foundries and stockyards of Chicago. The train didn't just carry people; it carried a culture, a sound. Muddy Waters boarded a version of this line in Clarksdale, Mississippi. Howlin' Wolf. Little Walter. They rode north with their guitars and their memories, and what they made in Chicago's South Side clubs would eventually become rock and roll. We've already crossed the Delta; those fields are behind us now. But the corridor itself — the Illinois Central's right-of-way — is still under our wheels.

Coming up ahead, the tiny city of Arlington — incorporated in 1876, the same year as the Battle of Little Bighorn a thousand miles northwest, the same year the railroads were already stitching the continent together at a pace that made the Indian Wars feel, to the men in Washington, like a tidying up. Arlington today has 264 people. The Illinois Central corridor running through it was already old when most of those residents' grandparents were born.

The bedrock here is still the same loess and Continental deposits we've been riding over since well before mi 540 — fine alluvium, gravel, sand, everything the Mississippi and its tributaries laid down across the Tertiary period, that vast sixty-six-million-year span between the end of the dinosaurs and the arrival of the first glaciers. It looks featureless, this land. And in one sense it is — no rock outcrops, no ridges, just fields. But that flatness is information. It means we're on the flood plain's higher edge, above the most recent alluvium but still sitting on the deep sedimentary record of a river system that once drained most of a continent. At around mi 560, something changes underground — the rock beneath us steps back in time, from Tertiary all the way to the Middle Eocene, roughly forty-nine million years ago. We won't see it. But it's there.

Carlisle County on our right, formed in 1886 — the very year Geronimo surrendered and the Apache Wars ended, the last chapter of armed Indigenous resistance in the West. Named for John Griffin Carlisle, Speaker of the House. Another thin county: under five thousand people, poverty rate over twenty percent, the same mix of soybeans and wheat and education-sector jobs that sustains most of this corner of Kentucky. The county seat, Bardwell, is a few miles east of us. What you won't see but what the soil knows: we're crossing into the zone where Middle Eocene sediments begin to appear at depth — sand, mud, clay, chalk laid down when this part of North America was subtropical, when sea levels were higher and warm shallow embayments reached far inland.

There's a particular kind of American poverty that doesn't look poor from a train window — just flat and quiet and orderly, green fields stretching to a tree line, a grain elevator on the horizon, a farmhouse set back from a county road. Carlisle and Hickman Counties together have fewer people than many Chicago apartment buildings. The counties that emptied were often the ones the migrants left — not for lack of land, but for lack of wages, for lack of safety. The Illinois Central's passenger service through here peaked around 1920, when the City of New Orleans and its predecessors were running daily. By then the Great Migration's first wave had already transformed Chicago's demographics. This stretch of track was as much a social artery as a rail line.

We've just crossed, invisibly, into a different chapter of deep time. The bedrock beneath us has shifted from the younger Tertiary loess into Middle Eocene sedimentary rock — about forty-nine million years old. Picture a warm, shallow sea, something like the modern Gulf of Mexico pushed much farther north, laid down when the continents had already roughly their present shape but the climate was considerably warmer. Sand, mud, clay, chalk: the slow settling of marine sediment across millions of years. None of it shows at the surface here — the Mississippi has buried it under alluvium — but the formation is down there, tilted gently, recording a world of early whales, ancestors of modern horses no bigger than a dog, and forests of subtropical trees across a North America without a Rocky Mountain rain shadow.

Ballard County now — slightly larger, slightly less poor than the counties we've been riding through. Still soybeans, still corn, still the Illinois Central corridor threading it north to south. What's coming, though, is something different. Just a few miles ahead, the land stops being Kentucky. It stops being the Mississippi watershed. We're approaching the confluence — the place where, in American geographic terms, the entire eastern half of the continent sorts itself out.

Cairo, Illinois sits just ahead of us at the junction of the Ohio and Mississippi Rivers — one of the most strategically located cities in North America. During the Civil War, Ulysses Grant used it as a staging ground for the campaign down the Mississippi. Lincoln called it essential. The rivers made it a chokepoint: whoever held Cairo held the gateway to the Confederate interior. But Cairo's history after the Civil War is a grimmer story — a city that couldn't escape the shadow of racial violence, that watched its Black population endure decades of documented terror before the Great Migration began draining the region of the very people who had built its economy. By the time the civil rights era arrived, Cairo was already in decline. Today it has fewer people than it did in 1850. The levees that were built to protect it now mostly surround a ghost of what it once was.

Off to the left — the Ohio River. Nine hundred and eighty-one miles of it, rising from Pittsburgh in the Allegheny foothills and sweeping southwest to exactly this point, where it meets the Mississippi. The Ohio drains half the Appalachians, the industrial Midwest, most of Kentucky and Tennessee. Everything north of us — Indiana, Ohio, western Pennsylvania — all of it flows to this seam. We're looking at one of the great hydraulic junctions of the continent.

The geology shifts again here, quietly. As we approach the confluence, the Cenozoic sedimentary rocks under us represent the broadest category — the last sixty-six million years of river deposition and marine sedimentation in the embayment that was once the northern reach of the Gulf of Mexico. These are not ancient ocean floors; they are the debris of a continent slowly eroding into itself, sorted by water, deposited in layers, waiting. The Ohio and Mississippi between them carry about five hundred million tons of sediment south every year. That sediment is the future rock record — the Cenozoic layer that geologists a hundred million years hence will interpret as "a vast river system draining a continental interior."

Cairo. This is the journey's great hinge. To the left, the city — named, implausibly, for Egypt, by men who thought the confluence of the Ohio and Mississippi echoed the Nile meeting its delta. Founded in 1818 as a territory, platted as a city in 1837, it sits at the absolute tip of a levee-bound triangle of land between two rivers. We are also crossing, invisibly but decisively, from the Lower Mississippi watershed into the Ohio River watershed. The water falling on the land behind us has been draining to the Mississippi all the way from Hickman County. The water falling on the land ahead of us drains to the Ohio. We've crossed a continental divide — not a mountain pass, not a ridge, just a subtle tilt of the land. And we've crossed into Illinois. We've crossed out of the South.

The Great Migration had a line. It wasn't legal, it wasn't on a map, but every Black Southerner who rode this train felt it: the moment the train crossed the Ohio River. Letters home described it — the release of tension, the dropping of the guard that had been maintained for hundreds of miles through Mississippi and Kentucky, the ability to breathe. James Baldwin wrote about the Ohio crossing as a kind of threshold. It wasn't safety — Chicago had its own violence, its own red-lining and its riots — but it was different. A different set of laws. A different set of fears. The Illinois Central brought hundreds of thousands of people across this crossing. We've just made it ourselves.

Cairo today is listed as one of the most economically distressed small cities in the United States. The population that was thirty thousand at its Civil War peak is now under two thousand. The levees still stand — they have to; without them the city would simply not exist, sitting below flood stage at the confluence of two rivers. The Illinois Central still passes through, but it doesn't stop. A city that was once essential to American geography has been left at the margin of American attention. What's remarkable isn't the decline — river-junction cities boom and bust with the technologies of their era — but the speed of it. Cairo peaked before the Civil War ended and has been falling ever since. The railroads that killed the river trade ran right through it and gave it nothing.

Cairo Junction ahead — the rail junction where lines split for different northward routes. We continue up the Illinois Central corridor. This junction once saw a tremendous throughput of freight and passengers; today the traffic is a fraction of its peak. The infrastructure remains: rails, switches, grade crossings. The frame of the old system, still in use.

We're in Pulaski County, Illinois now — one of the poorest counties in the state, poverty rate at twenty-five percent. The land cover here is split between developed land and crops, a rarity in this segment. And the geology beneath us is doing something remarkable: we're moving through Cenozoic sedimentary rocks, but heading toward something much older. By around mi 590, the bedrock will suddenly be Serpukhovian — 323 to 330 million years old. That's a jump of roughly forty million years of rock record vanishing from beneath us, an unconformity — a buried gap where the Pennsylvanian rock sits directly on older strata, with everything in between eroded away or never deposited. The Serpukhovian was the late Carboniferous, when vast coal swamp forests covered this part of North America. Illinois sits on some of the deepest coal seams in the world, much of it Pennsylvanian in age, laid down in those swamps. The fossils in the ground just ahead tell the story: Stigmaria ficoides, Archaeocalamites radiatus, Knorria imbricata — all plant fossils, the root systems and branching stalks of Carboniferous tree-ferns and horsetails thirty meters tall.

We're riding over rock now that is 323 to 331 million years old — Serpukhovian, late Carboniferous. Say that number slowly: three hundred and twenty-three million years. The Appalachians were being built then, colliding continents crumpling the crust to the east while here, in the interior, vast warm swampy lowlands spread across a tropical Illinois. Clubmosses forty meters tall. Dragonflies with wingspans of two feet. The oxygen content of the atmosphere was higher than today — which is part of why the insects could grow so large and why the coal seams those forests left are so thick. That coal — compressed over three hundred million years from those forests — powered the steel mills of Chicago and Gary, and the migration that rode this very railroad was headed straight for the jobs that coal and iron created.

Wetaug, ahead — a small populated place in Pulaski County. The name is likely of Native American origin, like so many place names along the Illinois Central corridor. The train doesn't stop. A grain elevator, a crossroads, the geometry of the grid.

Around mi 600 we'll encounter a specific named formation — the St. Louis Limestone, Visean in age, running from about 338 to 341 million years old. That's a touch older than the Serpukhovian we're crossing now, another step deeper into the Carboniferous. Limestone means shallow tropical sea: clear, warm, teeming with crinoids and brachiopods, the kind of marine invertebrate world that was already ancient when the first dinosaur evolved. The fossils found here — Griffithidella, a trilobite relative; Phillibole planucauda — date to the Devonian and early Carboniferous boundary, 358 million years ago. The same ridge of ancient seafloor that the Carboniferous coal swamps built upon. Layers on layers, each telling a different sea.

Dongola ahead — a village of 661 people in Union County. Named, like Cairo, with an exotic geographic flourish: Dongola is a city in Sudan, on the Nile. Nineteenth-century Americans naming their river-country towns after African cities were drawing an imaginative geography of water and commerce. The Illinois Central connected these small places to Chicago the way the Nile connected Sudanese settlements to Alexandria. The analogy was intentional, at least for the founders. For the Black families who rode north through Dongola in the 1920s and 1930s, the geography had a different resonance — a town named for Africa, in a land where they were building something new.

At the far edge of our segment, Union County, Illinois — sixty-seven percent developed land, a third forested, a shift from the pure cropland we've been riding through. The rock underfoot is now the St. Louis Limestone: Visean, between 338 and 341 million years old, the compressed floor of a warm Carboniferous sea. In southern Illinois, this formation can be up to five hundred feet thick. It's the kind of rock that makes good aquifer country, that limestone dissolves slowly in groundwater and leaves behind sinkholes and springs. The Mississippi Embayment's ancient shorelines ran somewhere near here. We're moving toward the Shawnee Hills — the land will begin to feel less flat, less purely agricultural. The forest is coming back. The Ozark foothills are in the distance. We've crossed the Ohio, crossed the South, crossed three hundred million years of rock. Chicago is still five hours north.
units.place: St. Louis Limestone / Union County, IL

units.text: The limestone under our wheels right now was a seafloor. Roughly 340 million years ago, this corner of Illinois sat beneath a warm, shallow inland sea — the kind of sea that left behind the St. Louis Limestone, a formation thick with the compressed remains of crinoids and brachiopods. What you see as flat cropland was once a tropical reef system. The sea is gone, the reef is rock, and someone planted soybeans on top of it. That's deep time made ordinary, which is exactly what southern Illinois does: it buries its astonishments under the mundane.

We're moving through the southernmost reach of Illinois now — a region people around here have called "Little Egypt" since at least the 1820s, a nickname that stuck partly because of the resemblance to the Nile's floodplain country, and partly because in the famine winter of 1831, northern Illinois had to come south for grain, the way the Biblical tribes went down to Egypt. The name carried. So did the poverty. Union County, where we started this segment, has a poverty rate above twenty percent — education and healthcare are the economic pillars, which is another way of saying the industrial economy never fully arrived and never fully left, and the gap has been filled with institutions. Soybeans grow in the fields. The forests — a third of the county — hold back the light.

Around milepost 610 we cross a geological seam — from the Visean-age St. Louis Limestone, which we've been riding since we entered this segment, into the Upper Pope Group: Serpukhovian rock, roughly 327 million years old. That's thirteen million years younger, and what it means on the ground is a shift from the evaporite-laced limestone of a retreating sea to a mixed package of sandstone, shale, and limestone that records the coastline moving back and forth — the sea advancing, retreating, laying down sand, then mud, then carbonate again in repeated cycles. Southern Illinois is a stack of these sea-pulses, each one entombed in rock. We cross the Ohio watershed divide somewhere near here too — water that falls east of this invisible line eventually reaches the Ohio River rather than the Mississippi. We've been in the Upper Mississippi drainage; now we're edging toward the Ohio's basin. The continent is sorting our rainwater for us.

A few miles to our left is the village of Alto Pass — 342 people at last count, which is fewer than in 2010. It sits near Bald Knob, one of the higher points in southern Illinois, where a large white cross has stood since 1963 — a local landmark visible for miles. Alto Pass itself was a railroad village, the kind of place that bloomed when a line needed a stop and thinned when the stops were rationalized away. The bedrock is shifting beneath us just ahead: we're about to cross off the St. Louis Limestone and onto something younger, stranger.

Makanda, to the left — 547 people, down slightly from 2010. In the early twentieth century it called itself the "Star of Egypt," leaning into that Little Egypt identity. It's the kind of name a small town adopts when it needs to mean something beyond its own limits. The Illinois Central Railroad made towns like Makanda possible, and the Illinois Central is the reason we're here at all: this line, the one we're riding, was the principal artery of the Great Migration. From the 1910s through the 1970s, Black families from Mississippi and the Deep South boarded these trains heading north — to Chicago, to industrial wages, to somewhere that was not the Black Belt's sharecrop economy. We're tracing that route in reverse, southbound, but the track is the same track.

The Illinois Central was chartered in 1851 and received one of the first great federal land grants — 2.6 million acres of Illinois public land, which it sold to fund construction. By 1856 it was the longest railroad in the world, a spine running from Chicago to Cairo at the southern tip of the state. It didn't intend to become the corridor of the Great Migration; it intended to carry grain north and manufactured goods south. But infrastructure is indifferent to intention. The same rails that moved coal and corn moved people. During World War One, when northern factories were desperate for labor and immigration from Europe had dried up, labor agents for northern companies sometimes boarded this very line in Mississippi, offering tickets and wages. The Chicago Defender — the Black newspaper that circulated covertly through the South, sometimes passed hand to hand because white postmasters would confiscate it — ran stories about life in Chicago alongside train schedules. The schedules were the promise. The train was the mechanism.

Carbondale. Our station stop here. We're pausing in the largest city in southern Illinois outside of the St. Louis suburbs — about 25,000 people, anchored by Southern Illinois University, which was founded as a normal school in 1869, four years after the Civil War. The city's name is blunt about what this region once was: coal country. Carbondale was platted in 1852, the year after the Illinois Central was chartered, and it grew because the railroad gave the coal a way out. The mines are largely gone now. The university stayed. Jackson County, where we sit, has a poverty rate of twenty-three percent — one of the higher figures in the state — and SIU is the dominant employer. Education replaced extraction. That's a pattern we'll see again.

Leaving Carbondale, the bedrock shifts again — into the Bashkirian stage, Morrowan in North American terminology, roughly 323 to 312 million years old. This is coal-measure rock: sandstone, shale, and coal laid down in the vast swampy delta forests of the Carboniferous. The coal seams of southern Illinois are Carboniferous in the most literal sense — carbon, preserved. Those ancient tree-fern forests, their wood compressed under hundreds of millions of years of burial, are what the mines here extracted. The name Carbondale is not metaphorical. The city is named for the rock beneath it. And the rock was named for an era — the Carboniferous, the coal-bearing — that this exact landscape helped define.

To the right, Hurst — a small city in Williamson County, incorporated in 1903. Williamson County has a different kind of history than the university towns. In the early 1920s it was the site of some of the most brutal labor violence in American history: the Herrin Massacre of 1922, when striking union miners killed strikebreakers imported to reopen a strip mine. Nineteen men died. The county was called "Bloody Williamson" for decades. The coal economy generated wealth and fury in roughly equal measure, and the landscape here still carries both: the reclaimed strip-mine land, the old company-town grid, the quiet that follows an industry's departure.

The Tradewater Formation lies under us now — Bashkirian rock from around 320 to 310 million years ago, shale and sandstone and coal and limestone, up to 650 feet thick in southern Illinois. All of this coal geology was discovered and exploited in a compressed historical window: the Illinois coal boom ran roughly from the 1870s through the 1950s. In that same period, the Great Migration was moving through on the rails above these seams. There's a connection that rarely gets made: the mining towns of southern Illinois were themselves labor frontiers, importing workers — often Black workers from further south — into dangerous, low-wage jobs. The migration north wasn't a single clean movement from oppression to freedom. For many families it was a multi-generational journey, with stops in coal towns, in company housing, in places like Williamson County, before Chicago. The Illinois Central carried them through. The rock underneath funded the track.

Ahead, Du Quoin — a city whose name carries a story in its spelling. Jean Baptiste de Coigne was a chief of the Tamaroa and later the Kaskaskia people during the American Revolutionary War, an ally of George Rogers Clark in the Illinois campaigns of 1778 and 1779. His name was French, which tells you about the colonial history layered through this region: French missionaries and traders arrived in the late 1600s, a century before the Americans, and left their language in the place names. Du Quoin was incorporated in 1853, platted on the Illinois Central line, and grew on coal. It's Perry County now, and Perry County sits in that southern Illinois stretch that locals have always called Little Egypt.

The bedrock under Du Quoin is Missourian — Gzhelian stage, roughly 306 to 304 million years ago, sandstone and shale and more coal. A first introduction is warranted: Missourian is a North American provincial stage of the Late Pennsylvanian period — a name derived from the Missouri region where these rocks were first systematically described. It's slightly younger than the Bashkirian coal measures we passed through around Carbondale and Hurst. These are all Carboniferous rocks, all deposited in the great equatorial swamp forests that covered what is now the American Midwest when it sat near the equator. Each formation is another pulse of swamp, another burial of carbon. Illinois is built on layered forests that never saw sunlight again.

The village of Tamaroa ahead takes its name directly from the Tamaroa people — the same indigenous nation that Jean Baptiste de Coigne led, the same people after whom Du Quoin is named at one remove. The Tamaroa were part of the Illinois Confederation, a group of Algonquian-speaking peoples who occupied this region before French contact, and were decimated afterward: by disease, by the Iroquois wars of the 1680s and 1690s, and by the slow erosion of land and sovereignty through the French and then American periods. By the early 1800s the Kaskaskia — the remnant nation that absorbed many Tamaroa — had ceded the last of their Illinois land. What remained were the names: Tamaroa, Du Quoin, Kaskaskia, Illinois itself. Names are the last thing to go.

We've been following the Illinois Central's original 1856 alignment through much of this segment — the same route surveyed through the land-grant corridor, engineered to link Chicago to Cairo by the most direct practicable line. The railroad didn't follow rivers here the way it did further south. Southern Illinois has no single navigable spine, so the engineers ran the line through the upland, threading between the watersheds, connecting coal fields to markets. The result is a route that feels slightly arbitrary from the window — towns appear and disappear, not clustered along a river valley but strung on the rail itself. The railroad was the valley. The towns grew where the stops were. Some of them are still here. Some of them thinned out when the stops moved or closed. That's the whole story of a railroad town, compressed into a drive-past.

Du Bois, Washington County — 175 people, another French name on the map, this one simply meaning "of the woods." We're at the edge of Washington County now, which has a markedly lower poverty rate than the counties we've been riding through — 8 percent, versus 20 to 23 percent in Union and Jackson. The industries here include manufacturing alongside education and health. The bedrock is shifting once more, into the Bond Formation — Kasimovian stage, around 305 to 304 million years old: shale, sandstone, limestone, coal. One more introduction: Kasimovian is the Late Pennsylvanian stage just above Missourian — named for Kasimov, Russia, where the type sections were described in the 19th century. Here it means more coal measures, another buried forest, another seam. Washington County extracted some of it. The rail carried it north.

Sixty miles covered. The geology has walked us from a 340-million-year-old seafloor through successive swamp forests and coal measures laid down over the next 35 million years — each formation a chapter in the Carboniferous encyclopedia that southern Illinois became. Above all of that rock, in historic time: Native nations dispossessed and renamed into place names; French colonizers who left their language but not their presence; the Illinois Central driving through and platting towns; the coal boom and the labor wars; and the trains moving north, carrying families from the Black Belt toward Chicago. We are somewhere in the middle of that last story still. The track we're on carried those passengers. The track is continuous. So is the story.

The rock under us right now is about 305 million years old — Kasimovian shale and sandstone, with thin seams of limestone and coal laid down when this whole region sat near the equator, in a shallow tropical sea. You can't see the bedrock from here; it's buried under glacial till and loess, the Illinois flatlands draped over ancient ocean floor. We're riding the spine of southern Illinois — "Little Egypt," locals call it, the triangular southern tip of the state, where the Ohio and Mississippi rivers converge. The name came partly from irony, partly from necessity: when northern Illinois crops failed in the 1830s, people came south to buy grain, the way the Israelites went to Egypt.

The Illinois Central Railroad — our corridor — was something remarkable when it opened in 1856: the longest railroad in the world at that moment, over 700 miles of continuous track from Chicago down to Cairo at the Mississippi's meeting with the Ohio. Congress had granted the IC over 2.5 million acres of federal land to finance it, the first such land-grant railroad in American history. That precedent — giving away the public domain to build private infrastructure — would go on to shape the entire West.

But what the IC really did, over the following century, was carry people. Specifically, Black families from the Mississippi Delta northward, decade after decade, from the 1910s through the 1960s. We're riding the physical backbone of the Great Migration. The tracks we're on now were the tracks those families rode — from Clarksdale and Greenwood and Jackson, up through Memphis, up through Cairo, up through exactly this stretch of southern Illinois, toward Chicago. The train we're on is one of the last descendants of those same northbound departures.

Richview — population 238, a cluster of rooftops and a water tower barely slowing before it's gone. Villages like this were platted all through southern Illinois in the railroad era, each one hoping the IC stop would make it a town. Most remained exactly what Richview is: a crossroads, a grain elevator, fields on every side. Not a failure, exactly. Just the arithmetic of how many towns a railroad town could support.

Here's a detail that tends to get lost in the broad story of the Great Migration: the Illinois Central didn't just carry passengers. It carried news. The Chicago Defender — at its peak the most widely read Black newspaper in America — was physically smuggled into the South aboard IC trains by the railroad's Black porters. In Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, it was illegal to distribute the Defender; white postmasters refused it. So the porters carried bundles in their baggage cars and passed them to contacts in the depots. The paper published train schedules, northbound fares, addresses of rooming houses in Chicago. It ran stories about wages, about the stockyards, about neighborhoods where a family might land. The railroad and the newspaper were, together, a kind of underground telegraph — and we have been riding that telegraph line for the last hundred miles.

Wamac — the name itself is a kind of small map. It was incorporated in 1916 and the name is a portmanteau of three counties: Washington, Marion, and Clinton. A tri-county town straddling political lines, born in the railroad and coal era. Southern Illinois sat on enormous coal seams — those Kasimovian layers we mentioned — and the early twentieth century here was coal country, with small shaft mines scattered across the region. By 1916, when Wamac incorporated, the mines were hiring. That same year, on the other end of this railroad, Chicago's Black population was beginning its rapid climb. The labor markets were connected, invisibly, by these tracks.

We're coming into Centralia — a scheduled stop. Named not for any geographic center but for the Illinois Central itself, which founded the town in 1853 as a division point and repair facility. If you're stepping off, Centralia is the stop. If you're staying aboard, we'll be here briefly.

Centralia's history carries one of the darkest dates in American mining. On March 25, 1947, an explosion tore through Centralia Coal Mine No. 5, killing 111 men. Investigators had warned the mine was dangerously gassy. Miners had written directly to the governor — twice — begging for inspection. The warnings were ignored. It was the same pattern that had killed miners in company towns across the country for decades: men who knew the danger, owners who calculated the risk as acceptable, and a government too close to industry to intervene. The Centralia mine disaster helped push through the Federal Mine Safety Code of 1947, the first meaningful federal mining safety law. A hundred and eleven men, most of them from this small city, paid for it.

We're crossing into Marion County now, and the land is flattening further. This county — county seat at Salem — has a poverty rate nearly double Washington County's, and it's been shedding population for decades. The economic story here is the same one playing across rural mid-America: manufacturing consolidated and moved, the mines closed, the farm economy requires far fewer hands than it once did, and what's left is the health and education sector — the hospital, the school district — as the largest employers.

Salem itself has a minor presidential footnote: William Jennings Bryan was born there in 1860. Bryan who ran three times for president on platforms of silver coinage and agrarian populism, who prosecuted John Scopes for teaching evolution in 1925, who gave the "Cross of Gold" speech in 1896 that electrified a Democratic convention. He was Marion County's most famous product — and his political career was a long argument, on behalf of exactly this kind of rural county, against the Eastern financial establishment that he believed was strangling it. The argument didn't win. The county's trajectory since suggests the forces he was fighting won instead.

Odin. Named, apparently, for the Norse god of wisdom — one of those nineteenth-century naming enthusiasms when classical and mythological place names scattered across the Midwest like seeds. A small farm town in the flat middle of Marion County. Soybeans and corn in every direction; the tree line has thinned considerably from the forested stretch we came through earlier.

Around mile 700 we'll cross from the Bond Formation into the Mattoon Formation — a subtler transition than it sounds. Both are Kasimovian, both are the same general mix of shale, limestone, sandstone, and coal seams. But the Mattoon is slightly younger, perhaps four to five million years younger, and in southern Illinois it can run up to 600 feet thick. These are sediments laid down in the same kind of cyclothem — those rhythmic alternating layers of coal and marine rock that record a world where sea levels rose and fell repeatedly as Gondwana's glaciers advanced and retreated, a hundred million years before the first dinosaur. We're not just riding across Illinois. We're riding across the margins of an ancient sea, its rhythmic breathing recorded in the stone below us.

Tonti — named for Henri de Tonti, the Italian-born lieutenant of La Salle who explored the Illinois country in the 1680s and helped establish French influence in the interior of North America. Tonti was known as "Iron Hand" because he'd lost a hand in a grenade explosion in Europe and wore an iron prosthetic. He helped build Fort Crevecoeur on the Illinois River, negotiated with Native nations across the Great Lakes and Mississippi Valley, and outlasted La Salle — who was murdered by his own men in Texas in 1687. The Midwest is thick with French colonial names that most travelers pass without registering: Tonti, Joliet, Peoria, Des Moines, Detroit. Each one a residue of a French empire that lasted 150 years and then vanished.

The counties we're passing through now were part of a quieter demographic story that ran alongside the Great Migration: the movement of poor white families out of southern Illinois and southern Indiana toward Chicago, Detroit, and the industrial cities of the Great Lakes. The Dust Bowl accelerated it in the 1930s, but it had been building since the mines began closing in the 1920s. "Hillbilly Highway" is the name sometimes given to U.S. Route 41, which ran roughly parallel to the IC corridor — white Appalachian families moving north in the same years, on the same roads and rails, for the same economic reasons, into some of the same neighborhoods. The two migrations rarely appear in the same sentence in popular memory. On the ground, they overlapped.

Alma — another small Marion County settlement in the corn and soybean flatness. The forest cover that defined the first part of this segment has nearly disappeared. What we have now is the open Midwest grid: section-line roads running perfectly north-south and east-west, fields that go to the horizon, grain bins catching the light. The Interior River Valleys and Hills ecoregion is giving way, mile by mile, to something more open, more regularized by agriculture. Ahead, past mile 760, we'll cross into the Central Corn Belt Plains — flatter still, the great agricultural engine of the continent.

The Mattoon Formation under us now was named for Mattoon, Illinois, about forty miles north of here — a town that achieved brief national notoriety in 1944 when a local newspaper ran a story about a "mad gasser" who was supposedly releasing a paralyzing gas through residents' windows at night. Dozens of people reported symptoms: nausea, paralysis, a sweet smell in the air. The FBI investigated. Illinois state health officials investigated. The conclusion, eventually, was that no gasser existed — that the reports were a case of mass psychogenic illness, anxiety in a town depleted by wartime absences feeding a real physical symptom. It became a textbook case in the study of mass hysteria, still cited in psychology literature today. A formation named for a town, and the town's most famous moment is a collective hallucination in a time of war. History is strange that way.

Farina — the only town of that name in the United States, which is a remarkable distinction for a village of 540. The name means flour, or meal, in Latin and Italian, appropriate for a county that grows grain. Farina sits on the line between Marion and Fayette counties. Small as it is, it's precisely the kind of place the Illinois Central created and then slowly outlasted: a flag stop, a grain elevator, a Main Street that had its moment and then contracted as the car replaced the train and the Interstate replaced the local highway.

We're approaching a watershed boundary that most passengers never notice but that mattered enormously to the people who mapped and settled this country. Around mile 720, we'll cross the divide between the Mississippi watershed and the Ohio watershed — two of the great river systems of North America, whose division runs through the middle of southern Illinois. Rain that falls on one side of that line flows west to the Mississippi; rain that falls on the other flows east and south to the Ohio, then to the Mississippi below Cairo. The two watersheds converge only at that single point — at the bottom tip of Illinois, where the rivers themselves finally join.

The Illinois Central's route crossed that divide deliberately. The railroad's planners understood that controlling the main north-south corridor across both watersheds meant controlling the interior of the continent. In the 1850s, when the IC was built, this was not a metaphor — it was a military and commercial fact. The Union Army would use these tracks to move troops and supplies during the Civil War. Grant's campaigns in the western theater depended on the IC. What we're riding was, in the 1860s, a strategic military asset, and the divide we're about to cross was part of what made it one.

Edgewood — 398 people, just over the county line into Effingham. The name signals the edge of something, the transition we're in the middle of: forest giving way to cropland, southern Illinois giving way to central Illinois, the Interior River Valleys ecoregion shading toward the Corn Belt ahead. Effingham County's land cover is 67% developed — a significant shift from the forested and agricultural mix behind us. The county seat of Effingham is a crossroads town, where Interstate 57 and Interstate 70 intersect, which is really to say where the north-south corridor and the east-west corridor cross. We built highways on top of the same logic that sited the railroads: the same passes, the same low ground, the same drainage that made movement easy. The corridor endures. The technology changes.

Over the next two to three hours, the land will continue its subtle lift — about two hundred feet of elevation gain across the next 150 miles — and the character of the country will shift from the forested, coal-seamed hills of "Little Egypt" toward the open, flat geometry of the Central Corn Belt. The Illinois Central's great northbound corridor keeps pulling us toward Chicago, as it has pulled travelers and migrants for 170 years. Every mile we gain is a mile more the passengers of the Great Migration rode, carrying their whole lives in suitcases and boxes, watching this same flat country unroll outside the window, trading one world for another.

Small towns along the Illinois Central earned their names in a particular way: a railroad official liked you, or you had the deed to something the line needed. Mason up ahead is one of those — named for Roswell Mason, an Illinois Central superintendent who later became mayor of Chicago during the Great Fire. Three hundred people live here now. The town platted in 1865, the same year the war ended and the railroads began their real work of stitching the continent. The Central didn't just run through these towns. It made them, and unmade others, and the choice of which was which often came down to one man's name on a deed.

The Illinois Central wasn't only a freight road or a settlers' road. By the early twentieth century it had become something else entirely — the single most consequential route in the story of African American migration out of the South. The Chicago Defender, the great Black newspaper, was smuggled south on Illinois Central trains; Pullman porters passed it hand to hand. Families in Mississippi read it and made plans. They rode this very line north — through the Delta, up through Cairo at the confluence, then straight north across this Illinois flatland toward Chicago. Sociologists would later call it the Great Migration. The people who lived it called it going north, or going to Chicago, or just leaving. Between 1910 and 1970, roughly six million people made that move. The Illinois Central carried hundreds of thousands of them, sitting in the cars, watching the fields change, watching the country open up. We're riding the same iron right now.

The land outside — beans and corn stretching flat to the horizon — sits on the Mattoon Formation, a Pennsylvanian-age sequence laid down roughly three hundred million years ago when this place was a vast coastal swamp at the edge of a shallow inland sea. What you're seeing is the eroded top of that world: shale, limestone, thin coal seams, sandstone, all buried under glacier-scraped till. Effingham County, county seat just south of us, is the commercial center for this stretch of south-central Illinois. Median income above seventy thousand. Manufacturing and health services. Soybeans and corn. It looks permanent. The rock underneath it says otherwise — this land has been sea floor, coal swamp, glacier bed, and farmland, in that order.

The flatness here is the product of ice, not river. The great Illinoian glaciation — a continental sheet that covered most of the state — moved through perhaps 130,000 years ago, scraped the land toward level, and left behind the till plain we're crossing. The glacier is gone. What it left is this: a nearly perfect agricultural surface, gently drained, deep-soiled, tilted just enough that water moves. Illinois grows more soybeans than almost any other state. The logic is in the ground itself.

We're slowing into Effingham — a real stop, passengers on and off. The station sits at the crossing of Interstate 57 and Interstate 70, which meet here in a famous interchange locals call the Cross of Illinois. Two of the country's major interstates, perpendicular at this small city. Before the highways it was the Illinois Central and the Baltimore and Ohio. Before that, wagon roads. The place has been a crossing for as long as there have been crossings. That's not coincidence — the topography funnels movement through here, a gentle ridge between watersheds. The town is 34,000 people now, a regional junction for southern Illinois. We'll be moving again shortly.

The year 1865 keeps appearing in this segment — Mason platted it, Effingham County reorganized after it. That's because the end of the Civil War didn't just free four million people; it released an enormous pent-up energy of movement. Soldiers discharged. Freedpeople leaving plantations. Railroad land grants activated. Towns platted on speculation. The Illinois Central had received one of the largest federal land grants in history — 2.5 million acres along its right-of-way — and it was selling that land aggressively, running ads in German and Scandinavian newspapers to attract immigrant farmers. Much of this country was settled in the decade after Appomattox by people who came specifically because the railroad offered them land on credit. The fields we're watching out the window right now may well trace their original survey lines to that moment — a land office clerk in 1866, a German family newly arrived, a forty-acre plot that became a farm that became the corner of a county road.

Sigel, ahead — a small town of about 330, named after Franz Sigel, the German-American Union general whose name was famous enough in 1867 to sell lots. German immigrants named dozens of Illinois towns after him in that period; he was the Lincoln of the German-American community, proof that their people had fought on the right side and belonged here. The town never grew large. It didn't need to — it was a market town for the surrounding farms, and the farms were what mattered. The railroad gave it a reason to exist; the railroad also ensured it stayed small by giving the same access to every other town within fifteen miles.

The fossils in the bedrock under our wheels right now include brachiopods, corals, and mollusks from that 304-million-year-old Pennsylvanian sea. Lophophyllidium proliferum — a colonial coral — Derbyia crassa, a thick-shelled brachiopod — Neochonetes granulifer, a smaller one. They died on a sea floor that is now buried under two hundred feet of glacial till and topsoil. If you drilled down through the corn roots and the clay and the gravel and the older clays, you'd eventually hit limestone full of these creatures. They don't care that Illinois Central tracks run overhead. They've been here three hundred million years. We've been here for a geological instant.

Neoga — population around 1,400, though it's been shrinking since 2010. Platted in 1856, in the middle of the California Gold Rush decade, when the country was in a speculative fever about the West even as the Midwest was being quietly settled. The town sits in Cumberland County, part of the Charleston–Mattoon metro area. It has the characteristic profile of a central Illinois small city: schools, a grain elevator or two, a Dollar General, a diner that's been there since before any of us were born. What Neoga has that most don't is a name — the origin unclear, possibly a corruption of a Native American word, possibly a railroad surveyor's invention. The Illinois Central ran through here, and the name stuck.

Think about what this flatland looked like to a family riding north from Mississippi in 1920. They'd left the Delta — the cotton fields, the debt, the daily threat of violence. They'd crossed the Ohio. And now this: Illinois, the Land of Lincoln, and it looks exactly like Mississippi from the window. Flat. Agricultural. Fields stretching to the horizon. Some families reportedly felt a confusion, even a disappointment, expecting the North to look different. It doesn't, not yet. Chicago is still a hundred and fifty miles north. The great industrial city is invisible from here. What's visible is the same flat agricultural logic they'd just left, except without the apparatus of the cotton system pressing down on it. The difference wasn't in the landscape. It was in the law, and the wages, and the possibility — contingent, partial, contested — of something better. That gap between what the land looked like and what it meant is one of the defining American ironies of the twentieth century.

Magnet — not a town, technically; an unincorporated community, which means no mayor, no city council, no incorporated limits. Just a cluster of buildings that grew up along the railroad south-southwest of Mattoon, and a name someone gave it. Unincorporated communities like this one are the substrate of rural Illinois — the places too small to form governments but real enough to show up on maps. They're usually older than their incorporated neighbors; they predate the legal infrastructure. Magnet probably had a grain platform, maybe a post office. The railroad defined it. When the railroad's business shrank, Magnet shrank with it.

Coles County, which we're entering now, has a poverty rate nearly twice what we've been passing through — 19 percent, against 10 percent in Effingham County. That's Eastern Illinois University in Charleston, the county seat; college towns often show high poverty rates because students count in the census. But it's also something else, a pattern visible across the Illinois Central corridor: the farther from the major interchange, the thinner the economic margin. The towns that the railroad made in 1856 and 1865 grew on the logic of agricultural service — elevating grain, shipping livestock, supplying farms. When that logic automated and consolidated, the towns that depended on it thinned. Charleston has the university to anchor it. Mattoon, ahead, has industry. The communities between them have the fields and the memory of what the railroad used to mean.

Mattoon is a real station — flag stop on the City of New Orleans, regular stop for the Illini and Saluki. The station itself dates to 1918, a handsome structure that's on the National Register of Historic Places. But the town's railroad history goes back to 1855, when the Illinois Central and the Terre Haute & Alton railroads crossed here — another crossing town, another place where the geometry of lines created a town. Mattoon has about 17,000 people today, and it's held on better than many Illinois Central towns. Decatur Meatpacking, Consolidated Grain, a manufacturing base that survived the farm crisis of the 1980s. The station is a reminder that these weren't just whistle-stops — Mattoon was a division point, a place where crews changed and locomotives took water and families came to meet arriving relatives from Chicago or from Memphis.

Here, near milepost 760, something shifts in the land itself — and it's worth naming. We're crossing out of the Interior River Valleys and Hills ecoregion and into the Central Corn Belt Plains. The Interior River Valleys are what they sound like: land shaped by rivers, carved and deposited by moving water, with some roll and variation in the terrain, a certain old-drainage irregularity. The Central Corn Belt Plains are something different. This is the prairie as agricultural system — flatter, more regular, engineered at landscape scale. The tile drainage systems running under these fields represent one of the largest hydraulic engineering projects in American history, invisible and mostly unappreciated. Farmers dug clay tile drains starting in the 1860s and 1870s, lowering the water table to make the wet prairie farmable. Without them, this land would be too waterlogged to plow. With them, it became the most productive agricultural surface on earth. The flatness you see isn't just geology. It's a century and a half of human management, tile by tile, acre by acre.

Humboldt — 361 people, platted in 1878, named after the great German naturalist Alexander von Humboldt, whose influence on American scientific culture in the nineteenth century was enormous. A dozen American towns bear his name. He never came here; he didn't need to. His Cosmos, the attempt to write a unified natural history of the planet, sold widely in English translation, and American settlers in the 1870s were naming things after him the way an earlier generation had named things after Washington and Lafayette. The town is small now, a village in the Coles County agricultural grid. But someone in 1878 reached for something grand when they named it — a place in a flat Illinois field carrying the name of the man who tried to understand everything.

Around milepost 770 we cross a continental divide — not the famous one in the Rockies, but the subtler one that runs across central Illinois, separating the Ohio-Mississippi watershed from the Upper Mississippi watershed. Water that falls south of this line drains generally southeast toward the Ohio and then to the Gulf. Water that falls north of this line drains north toward the Illinois River and then the Mississippi above its confluence with the Ohio. It's not a ridge you'd notice — the elevation change across the divide is measured in feet, not hundreds of feet. But it's a real boundary in the hydrology of the continent, and we're crossing it now. Ahead, at milepost 780, the bedrock changes too — from the Pennsylvanian Mattoon Formation, those 300-million-year-old Carboniferous swamp sediments, into older Paleozoic rock. The Paleozoic spans 541 to 252 million years ago — that's the whole era of ancient marine life before the dinosaurs. The rock ahead formed in a world with no land plants, no insects, no vertebrates on shore. Older and stranger than what we've been riding over.

Galton — another unincorporated community, this one in Douglas County, on US Route 45 four miles south of Arcola. Douglas County is slightly more prosperous than Coles — median income of 67,000, poverty rate below 10 percent. Soybeans and corn again; education and manufacturing. The county seat is Tuscola, a few miles north. We're approaching the edge of this segment, the edge of Coles County and the entry into a different geological chapter. The land ahead, in the Paleozoic rock, carries fossils of a different world — Devonian corals and mollusks from 393 million years ago, a time when this part of the continent lay under a warm tropical sea. Three hundred million years before the Illinois Central. Four hundred million years before us.

The Illinois Central ran a particular kind of train called the City of New Orleans — which is what this train's route descends from — and Arlo Guthrie wrote a song about it in 1971. Steve Goodman wrote it first, actually, dying of leukemia, and handed it to Guthrie, who made it famous. The song is an elegy for a train route and a way of traveling, for the conductors and gamblers and mothers with their children, for the towns the train calls at in the night. "Good morning, America, how are you?" It's a song about this corridor — this specific line, these specific flat fields, the long run from New Orleans to Chicago through the Illinois heartland. We're riding inside that song right now. The towns have thinned. The railroad has contracted. But the line still runs, and we're on it, moving north through the Paleozoic, toward Chicago, the way a hundred thousand migrants moved before us, toward something that looked, from down south, like a future.

The fields stretching away on both sides are growing the same two crops they've been growing since the glaciers left: corn and soybeans. Douglas County, seat at Tuscola — population under twenty thousand, tight and self-contained. What you're looking at is one of the most productive agricultural counties in the world, sitting on thirty feet of glacial till deposited ten thousand years ago.
