The bedrock beneath us is Paleozoic — limestone and shale laid down in warm shallow seas that covered this continent before there were any land animals at all. We ride on top of all that time like it isn't there.

The Illinois Central Railroad — the line we're traveling — was built through here in the early 1850s, and the towns that exist along this corridor mostly exist because of it. The IC ran straight north-south like a surveyor's line, which is exactly how it was designed. Congress granted the railroad two and a half million acres of Illinois land in 1850 — the first federal land grant for a railroad in American history. The deal was simple: the railroad would build, and in exchange it could sell alternate sections of land along the route to pay for construction. The towns platted along this line were land-grant towns. Settlers came not because the land was different here — it was all the same flat, rich prairie — but because the railroad had arrived and with it a market. Tuscola, Villa Grove, Champaign itself — all railroad towns, all mid-1850s, all dependent on the same iron thread we're following north.

Hayes is a dot on the map rather than a town — a cluster of structures that marks where a post office once stood, where grain moved through, where a name got attached to a location. The Central Corn Belt keeps these small nodes, these minimal settlements. Not every one of them had a story arc; some just persisted at half-volume.

The bedrock shifts under us around milepost 790 — nothing visible at the surface, everything buried under glacial drift, but something worth knowing about. We're crossing onto the Muscatatuck Group, a sequence of limestone, dolostone, and sandstone laid down in the Eifelian stage of the Devonian period. Eifelian: roughly 393 million years ago. To put that in scale — at that moment, the first forests hadn't appeared yet. There were fish with jaws, primitive amphibious creatures beginning to test the land, coral reefs in the shallow tropical sea that covered what is now central Illinois. The Muscatatuck Group includes the Grand Tower Limestone — reef rock, warm-water carbonate, now a few hundred feet below these corn rows. A reef. Right here. Three hundred and ninety-three million years is a long way from soybeans.

Pesotum — another small Champaign County node, population in the hundreds, platted as the railroad came through. The name is from an Algonquian word; the land was Potawatomi and Kickapoo country before American settlement arrived. The Illinois Central's corridor runs right through the heart of what had been the domain of Indigenous peoples who were removed by treaty and force in the 1830s, just twenty years before the railroad followed the same geography. The route the railroad engineers chose — straight, flat, minimal grade changes — was possible because Native peoples had already understood this landscape for centuries and had worn the travel paths that the surveyors later mapped.

We're now well into Champaign County — the largest county by population on this segment, home to the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. But the story the leg spine keeps returning to is not the university; it's the Illinois Central as the spine of the Great Migration. The IC ran from New Orleans north through Memphis, through Cairo at the southern tip of Illinois, up through Centralia and Champaign and on into Chicago. African Americans leaving Mississippi and the Deep South after World War One didn't choose this route randomly. They chose it because it was direct, because it had daily service, and because Chicago — specifically the South Side, specifically Bronzeville — was at the end of the line. The railroad didn't just move freight. It moved two million people north over fifty years. This flat stretch of Illinois we're crossing was not the destination; it was the passage. The land through the window tells you nothing about that. The rails beneath us tell you everything.

Savoy, a suburb of Champaign now — the metropolitan area has grown out to meet it. The Willard Airport, the Champaign-Urbana commercial airport, sits just south of here. There's a long history of aviation infrastructure along this corridor; Rantoul, a few miles north, had Chanute Air Force Base, one of the major training installations of the twentieth century. The flat land that made agriculture so productive made aviation equally viable — nothing to build around, nothing to navigate.

Champaign station is coming up. The city and Urbana sit side by side, the county seat in Urbana, the commercial and railroad center in Champaign. The Illinois Central chose the Champaign alignment; the university, founded 1867, chose Urbana, a mile east. The two towns grew toward each other and never quite merged. That division — commercial rail corridor on one side, university and government on the other — is a recurring pattern in Midwestern college towns. The railroad makes one city; the land grant makes another; they coexist uneasily for a century and eventually the university wins demographically. Champaign County's population today is over two hundred thousand — nearly all of that is the metro area. The surrounding farmland supports maybe a few thousand more.

We're at Champaign station. If you're stepping off, you're in the heart of a Big Ten university city that sits squarely on the migration corridor. The Illinois Central depot here was a significant waypoint — passengers from the South arrived here, some staying, most continuing north. The poverty rate in Champaign County runs nearly nineteen percent, elevated by student population but also by persistent inequality in a city where the university's prosperity doesn't fully diffuse into the surrounding community. A familiar pattern along this line. The station is a brief pause; the rails keep pointing north.

What the landscape doesn't announce, and what the migration story requires us to name: the Illinois Central carried Black Southerners north, but it also carried the terror they were fleeing. The same railroad that moved people away from the Black Belt moved the Chicago Defender newspaper south — smuggled in the sleeping car porters' bags, passed hand to hand through Mississippi and Alabama. The Defender ran columns describing Chicago wages, Chicago neighborhoods, Chicago possibility. Southern white authorities tried to ban it. The porters distributed it anyway. The information network that drove the Great Migration ran on the same rails we're on. A newspaper going south, people going north, on the same train, through the same Champaign station we just left.

Thomasboro — a village of just over a thousand people in northern Champaign County. Small, agricultural, self-sufficient at the scale of a single zip code. Nothing here distinguishes it from a dozen similar nodes on this corridor, which is itself a kind of information. The homogeneity of the Central Corn Belt Plains isn't emptiness; it's the deep result of a landscape that was fully converted to agriculture and then stayed that way for a hundred and fifty years.

The bedrock is shifting again under us. Around milepost 820 we'll cross onto the New Albany Shale sequence — a different geological chapter, the Givetian stage of the Devonian, roughly 383 million years old. The New Albany Shale is significant. It's dark, organic-rich, deposited in a warm epicontinental sea that was becoming anoxic — low oxygen at the bottom — which is exactly what you need to preserve the organic material that eventually becomes petroleum. The New Albany Shale is an oil and gas source rock across much of the Illinois Basin. None of that is visible from the window — it's three hundred feet down — but the economics of rural Illinois have occasionally bent around it. There were oil booms in southern Illinois in the early twentieth century, all drawing from Devonian source rock not unlike what's beneath us now. The reef we passed at milepost 790, the anoxic sea we're approaching — the Devonian ocean covered all of this, came and went, and left its record in the dark layers below the glacial drift below the soil below the corn.

Off to the right: Rantoul. Population twelve thousand, and in the town's recent history, the enormous gravitational absence of Chanute Air Force Base. Chanute opened in 1917 as an aviation training field — one of the first in the country — and grew through two World Wars into a major technical training installation for the Air Force. At its peak it employed nearly ten thousand military personnel and civilians. The base closed in 1993 under the Base Realignment and Closure process. Rantoul spent the next decade figuring out how to be a town without its largest employer. The airfield is now Rantoul National Aviation Center — a general aviation airport on the footprint of what was once a major military installation. The hangars are still there. Some of the barracks are apartments now. A place remade by the departure of the thing that made it.

Rantoul's history intersects the Migration in a specific way. During World War Two, the Army Air Forces trained African American pilots at a handful of installations; the broader Air Force training system that Chanute supported was deeply segregated. The Tuskegee Airmen trained in Alabama, but their technical training — aircraft mechanics, radio operation — moved through Chanute in the 1940s after a protracted fight over whether Black trainees could attend at all. The same year the Illinois Central was carrying Black workers north to Chicago factories producing war materiel, Black airmen were training on the same flat Illinois landscape to fly combat missions in Europe. The war accelerated everything — the migration, the industrial demand, the contradictions. Rantoul was part of that acceleration and probably doesn't talk about it enough.

Paxton, county seat of Ford County, off to the left — a city of about four thousand, founded 1859. That year is worth sitting with: 1859 is the year of John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry, the year the Pike's Peak gold rush was drawing thousands to Colorado, the year the country was fourteen months from the first shots of the Civil War. Paxton was platted because the Illinois Central came through and the company needed a county-seat town at regular intervals to anchor land sales. The date of the town's founding is inseparable from the crisis the country was about to enter. The settlers arriving in 1859 to build on the prairie were not escaping history; they were being carried along inside it.

We also cross a watershed divide somewhere around milepost 820 — the boundary between the Ohio River watershed and the Upper Mississippi watershed. No ridge marks it, no visible change. The land is as flat here as everywhere else on this segment. But a drop of rain falling on one side of that invisible line drains eventually to the Ohio and down to the Mississippi below Cairo; a drop on the other side drains more directly into the Illinois River and the upper Mississippi system. The whole agricultural logic of the Midwest — its drainage tiles, its levee systems, its river towns — hangs on which way the water moves. The Great Migration used the Mississippi corridor north. The water under these fields has been doing that same thing, moving north and west, for ten thousand years.

Buckley, at the edge of Iroquois County — the only county in the United States named Iroquois, which marks the reach of an awareness, however distant, of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy in a landscape far from their homeland. Buckley itself is a village of under five hundred, celebrating its sesquicentennial in 2006, which puts its founding in 1856 — the railroad again, the land grant again, the pattern completing itself one more time. We're crossing into the northeast corner of Illinois now. The Indiana border is not far east. Chicago is still an hour and a half ahead. The flat land continues, the corridor continues, and the story the rails are carrying continues with it.

Out the right window, the fields run dead flat to the horizon — corn stubble and soybean rows striped across the plain as far as you can see. This is Artesia Township, carved out of Iroquois County in 1921. The flatness isn't random. We're sitting on glacial lake bed, the drained bottom of a shallow sea of meltwater left when the last ice sheet retreated, roughly twelve thousand years ago. The ice smoothed everything and left behind a till so rich in minerals that this soil produces among the highest corn yields per acre anywhere on Earth.

We're deep inside Iroquois County now — the only county by that name in the United States. The Iroquois were never a people of this prairie; the name came west with settlers who carried it from New York, a tag of nostalgia or habit pinned onto a landscape the Iroquois Confederacy never held. The actual inhabitants of this ground were the Potawatomi and, before them, the Mascouten and the Kickapoo — peoples of the Great Lakes and tall-grass fringe who were pushed west and then displaced again by the land-grant machinery that platted every township you're looking at. The Illinois Central built through here before the Civil War. It didn't just carry grain; it carried people. After 1915, it carried tens of thousands of Black southerners heading from Mississippi and Louisiana toward Chicago — the Illinois Central as the literal iron spine of the Great Migration. We've been riding that spine all day.

Off to our left — that's Gilman, platted in 1857 when the Illinois Central was brand new iron and every town along it was a gamble on the future. Look at the grain elevator, that tall concrete tower at the edge of town: the railroad made Gilman, and the elevator made the railroad make sense. Corn and soybeans grown out here fed Chicago's meatpacking yards — the animal protein factory of the nation. Gilman sat at that chain's first link. The town is quiet now, population under two thousand, but the elevator still stands and the trains still pass.

Around milepost 850 the bedrock beneath us shifts — quietly, invisibly, since it's buried under a hundred feet of glacial drift — but shifts decisively. We've crossed from undifferentiated Paleozoic sedimentary rock into the Silurian System: dolostone, limestone, and shale laid down roughly 432 to 445 million years ago, during a time called the Llandovery. This is the first time on our journey we've ridden over Llandovery rock, so it deserves a moment. The Llandovery was an epoch of warm, shallow tropical seas — this latitude sat south of the equator, bathed in clear water. Coral reefs grew here. Trilobites crawled the seafloor. Among the fossils that turn up in these beds: Calymene breviceps, a trilobite; Cheirurus niagarensis, another. The Illinois state rock — the Kankakee Dolomite — belongs to this very system. Four hundred and thirty million years of compression and chemical replacement turned that tropical limestone slowly into dolomite, swapping calcium for magnesium crystal by crystal. The farm fields above it have no idea what's beneath them.

Straight ahead, Ashkum — a village of about 750 people. The name comes from the Potawatomi, one of the few original place names to survive in Iroquois County. Most were replaced. Ashkum sat along an early mail route and then the railroad, the classic sequence: trail, then rail, then town, then the question of whether the town persists when the next transportation layer bypasses it. Ashkum persisted, barely. You'll notice the water tower before the buildings.

The fields between Ashkum and our next point are as close to featureless as land gets — and that featurelessness is itself a story. The glaciers didn't just flatten this ground; they drained it. This was once wet prairie, a mosaic of marsh and tall-grass dotted with potholes left by ice blocks. The wet prairie was nearly impossible to farm until the 1870s and 1880s, when drainage tile — fired clay pipe laid just below the surface in a grid — let farmers lower the water table and convert wetland to cropland. It was one of the largest wetland conversions in American history, done farm by farm, county by county, with no central authority, just the economic logic of corn prices and railroad access. The migratory birds that once stopped here in the millions have no memory of it.

Chebanse, platted in 1854 — the same year the Kansas-Nebraska Act blew open the slavery question and the country began its slow crack toward civil war. The name is likely Potawatomi in origin, meaning something close to "little duck." The town straddles the Iroquois-Kankakee county line and sits right at the edge of the Kankakee River's drainage. By 1854, the Illinois Central was already running through here, and the town grew around the depot. What happened next follows the pattern we've been tracing all day: the railroad brought settlers, the settlers planted corn, the corn went to Chicago, and Chicago grew into the city that the Great Migration would target sixty years later as the promised land of industrial wages and relative freedom. Every one of these small towns was a rung in a ladder that ended in Chicago.

There's a detail worth holding as we roll toward Kankakee. The Great Migration wasn't a single wave — it was two, separated by the Depression. The first ran roughly 1910 to 1930: half a million Black southerners, many of them sharecroppers and tenant farmers from the Mississippi Delta and the Black Belt, rode the Illinois Central north. The second ran 1940 to 1970: another five million. The Illinois Central advertised in Black newspapers — particularly the Chicago Defender, which was smuggled into the Deep South because white postmasters in Mississippi refused to distribute it. Pullman porters carried the Defender in their bags, dropping copies at stops down the line. The train was both the vehicle and the information network. It carried people and the knowledge that leaving was possible. We're riding the same track.

We're pulling into Kankakee — the only real city on this segment, county seat, population just over twenty-four thousand. The city sits on the Kankakee River, and its name is Potawatomi: it meant something like "swampy country" or "low boggy ground." The Kankakee River here is modest, but it drains a vast marshy system to the east — the Grand Kankakee Marsh, once one of the largest freshwater marshes in North America, now almost entirely drained and farmed. Kankakee was incorporated in 1853, a railroad town from birth. It grew into a mid-sized industrial center — furniture, stove manufacturing, paper goods. And it became a destination on the Migration route: a stopping point, or for many, the end of the line before Chicago.

The station stop gives us a moment. Kankakee's station has been here in various forms since the 1850s. What you won't see from the platform is what the city became by the mid-twentieth century: a place where the industrial promise of the north began to show its own cracks. Manufacturing jobs peaked, then contracted. Kankakee's poverty rate today sits at fourteen percent — higher than the Illinois average. The Migration brought people north toward opportunity; deindustrialization pulled the opportunity away. The geography of hope and disappointment is layered here, and the train passes through without lingering.

Left window — Bourbonnais, a village that takes its name from a French-Canadian trapper, Noel LeVasseur dit Bourbonnais, who wintered here in the 1830s with a Potawatomi wife. He settled in 1832 — one of the first permanent European settlers in Kankakee County. The French-Canadian and métis presence in this part of Illinois predates American settlement by generations; these were the fur-trade people who moved between worlds, married into Native communities, and left place names the later Anglo settlers mostly couldn't pronounce and eventually respelled. Bourbonnais: the French would say "boor-bun-AY." The town says "bur-BON-ee." Both names belong to different chapters of the same place.

We're moving now through the last stretch before the Chicago suburban fringe catches us. The bedrock below us remains that Silurian dolostone — the Kankakee Dolomite — and has been laid down in those ancient tropical seas. Consider the fossils in the packet: Oxyprora mesialis, a brachiopod from about 335 million years ago. Euconospira waterlooensis — a gastropod, a spiral-shelled sea snail, crawling the Silurian seafloor when this was open ocean and the nearest land was a low volcanic arc to the east. These are not abstractions. Every quarry in Kankakee County that ever cut stone for Chicago's buildings was pulling up the compressed remnants of that reef ecosystem. The limestone that lines the foundations of nineteenth-century Chicago buildings — the limestone under the sidewalks and the bridges — came out of this Silurian layer. The city is literally built on an ancient coral reef.

Ahead and slightly right — Monee Reservoir, a man-made lake in Will County. We've just crossed into Will County, and everything changes here, economically if not visually. Will County's median household income is over one hundred thousand dollars — nearly sixty percent higher than Kankakee County's, which we just left. The reservoir is a recreational amenity, a sign of suburban prosperity rather than agricultural necessity. The land cover is shifting too: we're moving from open cropland into the developed fringe. The Chicago metropolitan area is reaching south toward us.

Monee, ahead — a small village that sits at the leading edge of the Chicago exurb. The name is likely derived from a Potawatomi word; the place was a stopping point on an early mail route. Today it's a satellite community growing under pressure from Chicago's southward sprawl. In another hour we'll be threading through the full freight and passenger complexity of the Chicago approach — the merger of all those rail lines that the Illinois Central and its competitors built out across the continent over a century and a half. The migration route ends where the city begins. Or rather, it ends where the city was always going to be: at the southern shore of Lake Michigan, which we haven't yet seen but which we can almost feel from here, the cold air off the water beginning to mix into the wind.

The ground under us right now is ancient seafloor — Silurian dolostone and limestone, four hundred and thirty million years old, pressed flat by glaciers and buried under centuries of till. The glaciers left this land almost level, which is why the corn and soybeans stretch to every horizon. Near this stretch, paleontologists have pulled trilobites from the rock — Calymene celebra, Bumastus insignis — creatures that swam a tropical sea before there were fish with jaws. Chicago is built on that vanished ocean floor.

The Illinois Central Railroad built this line as a spine — New Orleans to Chicago, twelve hundred miles of steel connecting the Deep South to the industrial North. In the decades after World War I, more than a million Black Southerners rode these rails out of Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia. Not as tourists. As people leaving sharecrop poverty and the constant threat of violence, bound for the stockyards and steel mills ahead. The train they rode was sometimes called the City of New Orleans; the route they rode was called the Great Migration. We've been traveling its northern reach since Mississippi, and now, within thirty miles of Chicago, we're at the delivery end — the place where the migration arrived.

By the 1940s, the Illinois Central was the most important Black corridor in America. Pullman porters, who worked these very cars, became one of the first strong Black labor unions in the country. Their union — the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, founded in 1925 by A. Philip Randolph — took twelve years to win its first contract. Twelve years. The men who served meals and made beds on these trains became pillars of the Black middle class in Chicago. They sent their children to college on those wages. One of those children was Medgar Evers's generation.

Homewood. A brief stop — one of the last before Chicago's Union Station. This suburb sits in the outer ring of the city's great industrial watershed. In the early twentieth century, workers streaming off the Illinois Central here fanned out into the foundries and meatpacking operations that ringed the city. The median income in Will County, which we've just crossed out of, runs above a hundred thousand dollars today. Cook County, which begins just north of here, averages twenty thousand less and carries poverty rates twice as high. Two counties. One train line. The economic gradient the Migration carved is still legible in the numbers.

Harvey, coming up ahead, was platted in 1891 — the same decade the Pullman Strike convulsed the nation. The town's founder, Turlington Harvey, imagined it as a model temperance community, dry by design, with light industry and Christian order. It failed on his terms and survived on its own. By the mid-twentieth century Harvey was majority Black, part of the industrial South Side's outer sprawl. Today its population is around twenty thousand, its poverty rate substantially higher than the county average. The neat temperance dream and the gritty industrial reality diverge in almost every town along this line.

Ahead: Harvey. A city that has cycled through ambition and abandonment several times over. Founded in 1891 with utopian intentions — a sober, orderly workers' paradise. That lasted about a decade. What replaced it was ordinary: factories, rail yards, working-class neighborhoods that filled with migrants from the South through the mid-century decades. Harvey is a place where the Migration arrived and stayed, built institutions, churches, block associations — and then watched the factories close. The deindustrialization of Chicago's South Side in the 1970s and 80s hit places like Harvey as hard as anywhere in the Midwest.

George Pullman built his town — the one we're approaching — as an experiment in benevolent capitalism. The year was 1880. He'd made his fortune on the sleeping car: the Pullman Palace Car, first class overnight travel, the kind of luxury only available to people with money. But the men who cleaned those cars, who made the beds and served the meals, were almost exclusively Black — hired deliberately because Pullman calculated they would be deferential, recognizable to white passengers as servants, and grateful for the work after emancipation. He got the deference for a while. What he didn't plan for was the union.

The Pullman Strike of 1894 shut down railroads across the country. Eugene Debs led it. Grover Cleveland sent federal troops to break it. The strike was crushed, Debs went to prison, but the labor movement learned something about what collective action could cost and what it could win. The Pullman porters had to wait another thirty years — until 1937 — to get their contract. But they got it.

Out the left window: the Pullman neighborhood, one of Chicago's 77 defined community areas. This is the company town George Pullman built from scratch in 1880 — brick rowhouses, a market hall, a library, a church, all designed by architect Solon Spencer Beman, all owned by the Pullman Palace Car Company. Workers rented from Pullman, shopped at Pullman's stores, attended Pullman's church. When the Depression of 1893 cut wages but not rents, they struck. The town Pullman built to prove that labor and capital could live in harmony became the site of one of the most important labor confrontations in American history. The brick houses are still there. They're a National Monument now.

Chicago in 1910 had about forty thousand Black residents. By 1970 it had over a million. That is what the Great Migration means in a single city — a twentyfold multiplication in sixty years. The Illinois Central was the primary artery. Chicago's Black Belt — the neighborhoods running south from downtown along State Street — grew street by street, block by block, as families arrived with a suitcase and a relative's address written on a slip of paper.

The South Side neighborhoods we're passing through now — Oakland, Kenwood, Douglas — were at the center of that transformation. They produced Louis Armstrong, Muddy Waters, Nat King Cole, Gwendolyn Brooks. The Chicago Blues was born here when Mississippi Delta musicians plugged in electric guitars in small clubs on 47th Street, because acoustic guitars couldn't be heard over the crowd noise. The music moved north on this train and then got louder. That's the migration in miniature.

Ahead, along the South Side lakefront: the site of the Lake Michigan High-Rises, a Chicago Housing Authority project completed in 1962 and demolished in 1998. They stood for thirty-six years. Built as a solution to the postwar housing shortage — modern, high-density, publicly funded — they became instead a concentrated geography of poverty and neglect. The federal government funded construction and then cut operating budgets. Chicago diverted maintenance money. The towers deteriorated faster than anyone officially acknowledged. By the 1990s they were symbols of a policy failure that had displaced and concentrated exactly the families the Great Migration had delivered to Chicago's promise. The implosion in 1998 was televised. The land is condominiums now.

In a few minutes, without any sign you'd notice from the window, we cross an invisible line. The continental divide between the Mississippi River watershed and the Great Lakes. Every drop of rain that has fallen to our south — across Mississippi, Tennessee, Kentucky, southern Illinois — drains eventually to the Gulf of Mexico, through the vast branching system of the Mississippi. Here, the drainage tips. Rain falling north of this threshold reaches Lake Michigan, then the St. Lawrence, then the Atlantic. Two oceans. One invisible ridge. We've been in the Mississippi's world for the entire journey. We're leaving it now.

This is the hydrological hinge of the continent, and we're crossing it right now. No mountain marks it. No river. The land is flat, the elevation barely changes — we've held near two hundred feet above sea level for a hundred and fifty miles. But the water under our wheels has been choosing different oceans for millennia. The Mississippi system drains roughly forty percent of the lower forty-eight states, a watershed so large that a raindrop falling in Montana can reach the Gulf of Mexico. What lies ahead of us — Lake Michigan, the Great Lakes, the St. Lawrence — is a separate world entirely. The journey that began in the Delta has, at this unmarked moment, crossed out of the Mississippi's long reach.

Chicago appears as a density that builds from south to north — first the scattered industrial buildings, then the expressway overpasses, then the grid of neighborhoods laid out with the rigidity of a place that had to absorb hundreds of thousands of people very quickly. The city's street grid doesn't acknowledge the lake or the rivers; it runs at a slight angle to the compass, oriented to the original land survey, which was laid down before the city existed.

The Illinois Central pulled into a lakefront station — the one we're arriving at has moved and been rebuilt several times. But the route itself, from the Delta to this city, has been the same iron thread for a hundred and fifty years. We rode it from Mississippi silt and sharecrop fields and the memory of Emmett Till, through Harvey and Pullman and the South Side, across the invisible divide between two oceans, into the second-most-populated county in the United States. The Great Migration didn't end when it arrived here. It became Chicago.

Chicago. Union Station ahead. The Illinois Central carried more people between the South and this city than any other single line in American history — millions of journeys, most of them one-way, most of them carrying everything a family owned. The city they arrived in was loud, cold, and often hostile. It was also genuinely transformative — in music, in literature, in labor politics, in American culture. What the train brought north was not just labor. It was a people who remade the city that received them. We've ridden the spine of that story. Step off into the noise of it.

lore.title: New Orleans Union Passenger Terminal
lore.summary: New Orleans Union Passenger Terminal (NOUPT) is an intermodal facility in New Orleans, Louisiana, US. Located at 1001 Loyola Avenue, it is served by Amtrak, Greyhound Lines, Megabus, and NORTA with direct connections to the Rampart–Loyola Streetcar Line.

lore.title: Pontchartrain Center
lore.summary: The Pontchartrain Center is a 4,600-seat multi-purpose arena in Kenner, Louisiana, United States. The facility opened in 1991. It hosts concerts and local sporting events.

lore.title: Norco, Louisiana
lore.summary: Norco is a census-designated place (CDP) in St. Charles Parish, Louisiana, United States. The population was 2,984 at the 2020 census. The community is home to a major Shell/Valero manufacturing complex. The CDP's name is derived from the New Orleans Refining Company.

lore.title: Manchac Swamp Bridge

lore.title: Ponchatoula, Louisiana

lore.title: Hammond, Louisiana
lore.summary: Hammond is the largest city in Tangipahoa Parish, Louisiana, United States, located 45 miles (72 km) east of Baton Rouge and 45 miles (72 km) northwest of New Orleans. Its population was 20,019 in the 2010 U.S. census, and 21,359 at the 2020 population estimates program.

lore.title: Independence, Louisiana

lore.summary: Osyka is a town in Pike County, Mississippi, United States. It is located on the Mississippi–Louisiana state line. As of the 2020 census, Osyka had a population of 381. It is part of the McComb, Mississippi Micropolitan Statistical Area. The peak of its population was in 1910.

Prattini, who bought it for his daughter, Annie and her husband George H. Terry. Their son, George B. Terry inherited the house and sold it in 1970.

lore.title: Trimble, Tennessee
lore.summary: Trimble is a town in Dyer and Obion counties in the U.S. state of Tennessee. As of the 2020 census, Trimble had a population of 547.

lore.title: Union City, Tennessee
lore.summary: Union City is a city in and the county seat of Obion County, Tennessee, United States. 11,170 people were living in the town as of the 2020 census. It is the principal urban settlement of the surrounding micropolitan area, which includes Obion County and Fulton County, Kentucky. Union City is home to Discovery Park of America which is a museum with many exhibits pertaining to local history, as well as state, national, and world history, science, technology, and art.

lore.title: Fulton, Kentucky
lore.summary: Fulton is a home rule-class city in Fulton County, Kentucky, United States. The population was 2,357 at the 2020 census, down from 2,445 at the 2010 census. It was once known as the "Banana Capital of the World", because 70% of imported bananas to the U.S. used to be shipped through the city. Fulton is part of the Union City-Hickman, TN–KY Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Water Valley, Kentucky
lore.summary: Water Valley is a census-designated place and former home rule-class city in Graves County, Kentucky, United States. The population was 235 as of the 2020 census. It was incorporated on April 19, 1884, and had its charter dissolved via court order effective June 20, 2016.

lore.title: Hickman County, Kentucky
lore.summary: Hickman County is a county located in the U.S. state of Kentucky. As of the 2020 census, the population was 4,521, making it the third-least populous county in Kentucky. Its county seat is Clinton. The county was formed in 1821. It is the least densely populated county in the state and is a prohibition or dry county.

lore.title: Arlington, Kentucky
lore.summary: Arlington is a home rule-class city in Carlisle County, Kentucky, in the United States. As of the 2020 census, Arlington had a population of 264. It was formally incorporated by the state assembly in 1876. Arlington is included in the Paducah, KY-IL Metropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Carlisle County, Kentucky
lore.summary: Carlisle County is a county located in the U.S. state of Kentucky. As of the 2020 census, the population was 4,826, making it the fourth-least populous county in Kentucky. Its county seat is Bardwell. The county was founded in 1886 and named for John Griffin Carlisle, a Speaker of the United States House of Representatives from Kentucky. It remains a prohibition or dry county. Carlisle County is included in the Paducah, KY-IL, Metropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Ohio River
lore.summary: The Ohio River is a 981-mile-long (1,579 km) river in the United States. It is located at the boundary of the Midwestern and Southern United States, flowing in a southwesterly direction from Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, to its mouth on the Mississippi River at Cairo, Illinois. It is the third largest river by discharge volume in the United States and the largest tributary by volume of the Mississippi River. It is also the sixth oldest river on the North American continent. The river flows through or along the border of six states, and its drainage basin includes parts of 14 states. Through its largest tributary, the Tennessee River, the basin includes several states of the southeastern United States. It is the source of drinking water for five million people.

lore.title: Cairo, Illinois
lore.summary: Cairo is the southernmost city in the U.S. state of Illinois and the county seat of Alexander County. A river city, Cairo has the lowest elevation of any location in Illinois and is the state's only city to be surrounded by levees. The city is named after Egypt's capital on the Nile and is located in the river-crossed area of Southern Illinois. It is coterminous with Cairo Precinct.

lore.summary: Cairo Junction — a populated place in Alexander County, None.

lore.title: Wetaug
lore.summary: Wetaug — a populated place in Pulaski County, None.

lore.title: Dongola, Illinois
lore.summary: Dongola is a village in Union County, Illinois, United States. The population was 661 at the 2020 census.

lore.title: Alto Pass, Illinois
lore.summary: Alto Pass is a village in Union County, Illinois, United States. The population was 342 at the 2020 census, a decrease from 391 in 2010. The Bald Knob Cross and Bald Knob Wilderness are nearby. Alto Pass lies roughly 5.1 miles to the northwest of downtown Cobden, Illinois. Illinois Route 127 runs just west of the village's downtown.

lore.title: Makanda, Illinois
lore.summary: Makanda is a village in Jackson County, Illinois, United States. As of the 2020 United States census, the population was 547, down from 561 in 2010. In the early 20th Century it used the slogan "Star of Egypt."

lore.title: Carbondale, Illinois
lore.summary: Carbondale is a city in Jackson County, Illinois, United States, within the Southern Illinois region informally known as "Little Egypt". As of the 2020 census, the city had a population of 25,083, making it the most populous city in Southern Illinois outside the Metro East region of Greater St. Louis.

lore.title: Hurst, Illinois
lore.summary: Hurst is a city in Williamson County, Illinois, United States. As of the 2020 census, Hurst had a population of 764.

lore.title: Du Quoin, Illinois
lore.summary: Du Quoin is a city in Perry County, Illinois, United States. Its name reflects an alternate spelling of the surname of Jean Baptiste de Coigne, a chief of the Tamaroa and later Kaskaskia indigenous people of the area during the American Revolutionary War and early statehood. As of the 2020 census, Du Quoin had a population of 5,827. It is best known for hosting the annual DuQuoin State Fair and the Street Machine Nationals.

lore.title: Tamaroa, Illinois
lore.summary: Tamaroa is a village in the Tamaroa Precinct of Perry County, Illinois, United States. As of the 2020 census, Tamaroa had a population of 544.

lore.title: Du Bois, Illinois
lore.summary: Du Bois is a village in Washington County, Illinois, United States. As of the 2020 census, Du Bois had a population of 175.

lore.title: Richview, Illinois
lore.summary: Richview is a village in Washington County, Illinois, United States. As of the 2020 census, Richview had a population of 238.

lore.title: Wamac, Illinois
lore.summary: Wamac is a city in Washington, Marion, and Clinton counties in the U.S. state of Illinois. The population was 985 at the 2020 census, down from 1,185 in 2010. Incorporated as a city on July 25, 1916, Wamac derives its name from the three counties.

lore.title: Tonti
lore.summary: Tonti — a populated place in Marion County, None.

lore.title: Alma

lore.title: Farina, Illinois
lore.summary: Farina is a village in Fayette and Marion counties, Illinois, United States. The population was 540 at the 2020 census. It is the only community with the name "Farina" in the United States.

lore.title: Edgewood, Illinois
lore.summary: Edgewood is a village in Effingham County, Illinois, United States. The population was 398 at the 2020 Census. Edgewood is part of the Effingham, IL Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Mason, Illinois
lore.summary: Mason is an incorporated town in Effingham County, Illinois, United States. The population was 323 at the 2020 census. It was named after Roswell Mason, an official of the Illinois Central Railroad. Mason is part of the Effingham, IL Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Effingham County, Illinois
lore.summary:
Effingham County is a county located in the south central part of the U.S. state Illinois. As of the 2020 census, the population was 34,668. Its county seat and largest city is Effingham.
Some other cities in Effingham County, Illinois include Altamont, Teutopolis, Beecher City, Montrose, Dieterich, Shumway, Watson, Mason, and Edgewood. Effingham County comprises the Effingham, IL Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Sigel, Illinois
lore.summary: Sigel is an incorporated town in Shelby County, Illinois, United States. The population was 329 at the 2020 census.

lore.title: Neoga, Illinois
lore.summary: Neoga is a city in Cumberland County, Illinois, United States. The population was 1,398 at the 2020 census, down from 1,636 at the 2010 census. It is part of the Charleston–Mattoon Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Magnet, Illinois
lore.summary: Magnet is an unincorporated community in Coles County, Illinois, United States. Magnet is located along a railroad line south-southwest of Mattoon.

lore.title: Mattoon station
lore.summary: Mattoon station is an Amtrak intercity train station in Mattoon, Illinois, United States. The station is a flag stop on the City of New Orleans route, served only when passengers have tickets to and from the station. It is a regular stop for the Illini and Saluki.

lore.title: Humboldt, Illinois
lore.summary: Humboldt is a village in Coles County, Illinois, United States. At the 2020 census, its population was 361. It is part of the Charleston-Mattoon Micropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Galton, Illinois
lore.summary: Galton is an unincorporated community in Douglas County, Illinois, United States. Galton is located on U.S. Route 45, 4 miles (6.4 km) north of Arcola.

lore.title: Rantoul, Illinois
lore.summary: Rantoul is a village in northern Champaign County, Illinois, United States. The population was 12,371 at the 2020 census. It is part of the Champaign–Urbana metropolitan area.

lore.title: Paxton, Illinois
lore.summary: Paxton is a city in and the county seat of Ford County, Illinois, United States. The population was 4,450 at the 2020 census.

lore.title: Buckley, Illinois
lore.summary: Buckley is a village in Artesia Township, Iroquois County, Illinois, United States. The population was 495 at the 2020 census. Buckley celebrated its sesquicentennial in 2006.

lore.title: Artesia Township, Iroquois County, Illinois
lore.summary: Artesia Township is one of twenty-six townships in Iroquois County, Illinois, United States. As of the 2020 census, its population was 854 and it contained 402 housing units. Artesia Township formed from portions of Ash Grove and Loda townships sometime prior to 1921.

lore.title: Gilman, Illinois
lore.summary: Gilman is a city in Douglas Township, Iroquois County, Illinois, United States. The population was 1,738 at the 2020 census.

lore.title: Ashkum, Illinois
lore.summary: Ashkum is a village in Ashkum Township, Iroquois County, Illinois, United States. The population was 750 at the 2020 census.

lore.title: Chebanse, Illinois
lore.summary: Chebanse is a village in Iroquois and Kankakee counties in the U.S. state of Illinois. The population was 1,044 at the 2020 census. The Kankakee County portion of Chebanse is included in the Kankakee-Bradley, Illinois Metropolitan Statistical Area.

lore.title: Kankakee, Illinois
lore.summary: Kankakee is a city in and the county seat of Kankakee County, Illinois, United States. Located on the Kankakee River, as of 2020, the city's population was 24,052. Kankakee is a principal city of the Kankakee-Bourbonnais-Bradley Metropolitan Statistical Area. It serves as an anchor city in the rural plains outside Chicago.

lore.title: Bourbonnais, Illinois
lore.summary: Bourbonnais is a village in Kankakee County, Illinois, United States. The population was 18,164 at the 2020 census.

lore.summary: Monee Reservoir — a reservoir in Will County, IL.

lore.summary: Monee — a populated place in Will County, None.

lore.title: Harvey, Illinois
lore.summary: Harvey is a city in Cook County, Illinois, United States. The population was 20,324 at the 2020 census.

lore.title: Pullman, Chicago
lore.summary: Pullman, one of Chicago's 77 defined community areas, is a neighborhood located on the city's South Side. Twelve miles from the Chicago Loop, Pullman is situated adjacent to Lake Calumet.

lore.title: Lake Michigan High-Rises
lore.summary: The Lake Michigan High-Rises, also known as Lakefront Homes, was a Chicago Housing Authority (CHA) public housing project in the North Kenwood–Oakland neighborhood located in the South Side of Chicago, Illinois, United States. Constructed in 1962 and completed in 1963, The Lake Michigan High-Rises originally consisted of four 16-story buildings, totaling 457 units. The Lake Michigan High-Rises was located west of Lake Shore Drive and was included as a part of the CHA Lakefront Properties. Today, only two buildings of the Lakefront Properties exist; they were officially renamed from Victor Olander Homes to Lake Parc Place in 1991. The other four high–rises were demolished by implosion in December 1998, it was the first and only to date in Chicago Housing Authority history.

co-58-22071-0.title: Orleans Parish, Louisiana
co-58-22071-0.summary: Orleans Parish is a parish of the U.S. state of Louisiana. Since 1870, the parish has been coterminous with the city of New Orleans, and the parish and city are largely governed as a single consolidated city.

co-58-22051-12.title: Jefferson Parish, Louisiana
co-58-22051-12.summary: Jefferson Parish is a parish in the U.S. state of Louisiana. As of the 2020 census, the population was 440,781. Its parish seat is Gretna, its largest community is Metairie, and its largest incorporated city is Kenner. Jefferson Parish is included in the Greater New Orleans area.

co-58-22095-24.title: St. John the Baptist Parish, Louisiana
co-58-22095-24.summary: St. John the Baptist Parish (SJBP) is a parish located in the U.S. state of Louisiana. At the 2020 census, the population was 42,477. The parish seat is Edgard, an unincorporated area, and the largest city is LaPlace, which is also unincorporated.

co-58-22105-48.title: Tangipahoa Parish, Louisiana
co-58-22105-48.summary: Tangipahoa Parish is a parish located on the southeastern border of the U.S. state of Louisiana. As of the 2020 census, the population was 133,157. The parish seat is Amite City, while the largest city is Hammond. Southeastern Louisiana University is located in Hammond. Lake Pontchartrain borders the southeastern side of the parish.

co-58-28113-96.title: Pike County, Mississippi
co-58-28113-96.summary: Pike County is a county located on the southwestern border of the U.S. state of Mississippi. As of the 2020 census, the population was 40,324. The county seat is Magnolia. Pike County is named for explorer Zebulon Pike. Pike County is part of the McComb, MS Micropolitan Statistical Area.

co-58-28085-120.title: Lincoln County, Mississippi
co-58-28085-120.summary: Lincoln County is a county located in the U.S. state of Mississippi. As of the 2020 census, the population was 34,907. Its county seat is Brookhaven. The county was created by the legislature on April 7, 1870, during the Reconstruction Era. It was formed from portions of Lawrence, Pike, Franklin, Copiah, and Amite counties. It was named for Abraham Lincoln, the 16th President of the United States. Lincoln County comprises the Brookhaven, MS Micropolitan Statistical Area, which is included in the Jackson–Vicksburg–Brookhaven Combined Statistical Area. The county is southwest of the state capital of Jackson.

co-58-28029-144.title: Copiah County, Mississippi
co-58-28029-144.summary: Copiah County is a county located in the U.S. state of Mississippi. As of the 2020 census, the population was 28,368. The county seat is Hazlehurst.

co-58-28049-168.title: Hinds County, Mississippi
co-58-28049-168.summary: Hinds County is a county located in the U.S. state of Mississippi. With its county seats, Hinds is the most populous county in Mississippi with a 2020 census population of 227,742 residents. Hinds County is a central part of the Jackson metropolitan statistical area. It is a professional, educational, business and industrial hub in the state. It is bordered on the northwest by the Big Black River and on the east by the Pearl River. It is one county width away from the Yazoo River and the southern border of the Mississippi Delta.

co-58-28051-252.title: Holmes County, Mississippi
co-58-28051-252.summary: Holmes County is a county in the U.S. state of Mississippi; its western border is formed by the Yazoo River and the eastern border by the Big Black River. The western part of the county is within the Yazoo-Mississippi Delta. As of the 2020 census, the population was 17,000. Its county seat is Lexington. The county is named in honor of David Holmes, territorial governor and the first governor of the state of Mississippi and later United States Senator for Mississippi. Holmes County native, Edmond Favor Noel, was an attorney and state politician, elected as governor of Mississippi, serving from 1908 to 1912.

co-58-28083-276.title: Leflore County, Mississippi
co-58-28083-276.summary: Leflore County is a county located in the U.S. state of Mississippi. As of the 2020 census, the population was 28,339. The county seat is Greenwood. The county is named for Choctaw leader Greenwood LeFlore, who signed a treaty to cede his people's land to the United States in exchange for land in Indian Territory. LeFlore stayed in Mississippi, settling on land reserved for him in Tallahatchie County.

co-58-28135-312.title: Tallahatchie County, Mississippi
co-58-28135-312.summary: Tallahatchie County is a county in the U.S. state of Mississippi. At the 2020 census, the population was 12,715. Its county seats are Charleston and Sumner.

co-58-28119-336.title: Quitman County, Mississippi
co-58-28119-336.summary: Quitman County is a county located in the U.S. state of Mississippi. As of the 2020 census, the population was 6,176, making it the third-least populous county in Mississippi. Its county seat is Marks. The county is named after John A. Quitman, Governor of Mississippi from 1835 to 1836 and from 1850 to 1851.

co-58-28143-360.title: Tunica County, Mississippi
co-58-28143-360.summary: Tunica County is a county located in the U.S. state of Mississippi. As of the 2020 census, the population was 9,782. Its county seat is Tunica. The county is named for the Tunica Native Americans. Most migrated to central Louisiana during the colonial period.

co-58-28033-384.title: DeSoto County, Mississippi
co-58-28033-384.summary: DeSoto County is a county located on the northwestern border of the U.S. state of Mississippi. As of the 2020 census, the population was 185,314, making it the third-most populous county in Mississippi. Its county seat is Hernando. DeSoto County is part of the Memphis metropolitan area. It is the second-most populous county in that statistical area. The county has lowland areas that were developed in the 19th century for cotton plantations, and hill country in the eastern part of the county.

co-58-47157-396.title: Shelby County, Tennessee
co-58-47157-396.summary: Shelby County is the westernmost county in the U.S. state of Tennessee. As of the 2020 census, the population was 929,744, and was estimated to be 910,226 in 2025, making it the most populous county in Tennessee and the 65th-most populous county in the United States. It is also the largest county in Tennessee in terms of geographic area. The county seat and the largest city is Memphis, a port on the Mississippi River and the second-most populous city in Tennessee and the 29th-most populous city in the United States. The county was named for Governor Isaac Shelby of Kentucky. It is one of only two remaining counties in Tennessee with a majority African American population, along with Haywood County. Shelby County is part of the Memphis metropolitan area. It is bordered on the west by the Mississippi River. Located within the Mississippi Delta, the county was developed as a center of cotton plantations in the antebellum era, and cotton continued as an important commodity crop well into the 20th century. The economy has become more diversified. It contains over 12.60% of the state's population.

co-58-47167-432.title: Tipton County, Tennessee
co-58-47167-432.summary: Tipton County is a county located on the western end of the U.S. state of Tennessee, in the Mississippi Delta region. As of the 2020 census, the population was 60,970. Its county seat is Covington. Tipton County, founded in 1823, is part of the Memphis, TN-MS-AR Metropolitan Statistical Area.

co-58-47097-456.title: Lauderdale County, Tennessee
co-58-47097-456.summary: Lauderdale County is a county located on the western edge of the U.S. state of Tennessee, with its border the Mississippi River. As of the 2020 census, the population was 25,143. Its county seat is Ripley. Since the antebellum years, it has been developed for cotton as a major commodity crop.

co-58-47131-504.title: Obion County, Tennessee
co-58-47131-504.summary: Obion County is a county located in the northwest corner of the U.S. state of Tennessee. As of the 2020 census, the population was 30,787. The county seat is Union City. The county was formed in 1823 and organized in 1824. It was named after the Obion River.

co-58-21075-528.title: Fulton County, Kentucky
co-58-21075-528.summary: Fulton County is the westernmost county in the U.S. state of Kentucky, with the Mississippi River forming its western boundary. As of the 2020 census, the population was 6,515. Its county seat and largest city is Hickman. The county was formed in 1845 from Hickman County, Kentucky and named for Robert Fulton, the inventor of the steamboat.

co-58-21105-540.title: Hickman County, Kentucky
co-58-21105-540.summary: Hickman County is a county located in the U.S. state of Kentucky. As of the 2020 census, the population was 4,521, making it the third-least populous county in Kentucky. Its county seat is Clinton. The county was formed in 1821. It is the least densely populated county in the state and is a prohibition or dry county.

co-58-21039-552.title: Carlisle County, Kentucky
co-58-21039-552.summary: Carlisle County is a county located in the U.S. state of Kentucky. As of the 2020 census, the population was 4,826, making it the fourth-least populous county in Kentucky. Its county seat is Bardwell. The county was founded in 1886 and named for John Griffin Carlisle, a Speaker of the United States House of Representatives from Kentucky. It remains a prohibition or dry county. Carlisle County is included in the Paducah, KY-IL, Metropolitan Statistical Area.

co-58-17077-624.title: Jackson County, Illinois
co-58-17077-624.summary: Jackson County is a county located in the U.S. state of Illinois with a population of 52,974 at the 2020 census, the county is located 98 miles southeast of St. Louis. Its county seat is Murphysboro, and its most populous city is Carbondale, home to the main campus of Southern Illinois University. The county was incorporated on January 10, 1816, and named for Andrew Jackson. The community of Brownsville served as the fledgling county's first seat. Jackson County is included in the Carbondale-Marion, IL Metropolitan Statistical Area. It is located in the southern portion of Illinois known locally as "Little Egypt".

co-58-17145-648.title: Perry County, Illinois
co-58-17145-648.summary: Perry County is a county in Illinois. According to the 2020 census, it had a population of 20,945. Its county seat is Pinckneyville. It is located in the southern portion of Illinois known as "Little Egypt".

co-58-17189-660.title: Washington County, Illinois
co-58-17189-660.summary: Washington County is a county located in the U.S. state of Illinois. As of the 2020 census, it had a population of 13,761. Its county seat is Nashville. It is located in the southern portion of Illinois known locally as "Little Egypt".

co-58-17121-684.title: Marion County, Illinois
co-58-17121-684.summary: Marion County is a county located in the U.S. state of Illinois. According to the 2020 census, it had a population of 37,729. Its county seat is Salem. Marion County comprises the Centralia, IL Micropolitan Statistical Area, which is included in the St. Louis-St. Charles-Farmington, MO-IL Combined Statistical Area.

co-58-17049-720.title: Effingham County, Illinois
co-58-17049-720.summary:
Effingham County is a county located in the south central part of the U.S. state Illinois. As of the 2020 census, the population was 34,668. Its county seat and largest city is Effingham.
Some other cities in Effingham County, Illinois include Altamont, Teutopolis, Beecher City, Montrose, Dieterich, Shumway, Watson, Mason, and Edgewood. Effingham County comprises the Effingham, IL Micropolitan Statistical Area.

co-58-17173-744.title: Shelby County, Illinois
co-58-17173-744.summary: Shelby County is a county located in the U.S. state of Illinois. According to the 2020 census, it had a population of 20,990. Its county seat is Shelbyville.

co-58-17029-756.title: Coles County, Illinois
co-58-17029-756.summary: Coles County is a county in Illinois. As of the 2020 census, the population was 46,863. Its county seat is Charleston, which is also the home of Eastern Illinois University.

co-58-17041-780.title: Douglas County, Illinois
co-58-17041-780.summary: Douglas County is a county located in the U.S. state of Illinois. As of the 2020 United States census, the population was 19,740. The county seat is Tuscola.

co-58-17019-792.title: Champaign County, Illinois
co-58-17019-792.summary: Champaign County is a county in the U.S. state of Illinois. As of the 2020 Census, its population was 205,865, making it the 10th-most populous county in Illinois. Its county seat is Urbana.

co-58-17053-828.title: Ford County, Illinois
co-58-17053-828.summary: Ford County is a county located in the U.S. state of Illinois. According to the 2020 United States census, it had a population of 13,534. Its county seat is Paxton. Ford County was part of the Champaign-Urbana Metropolitan Area until 2018, when the Office of Management and Budget removed the county from the area.

co-58-17075-840.title: Iroquois County, Illinois
co-58-17075-840.summary:
Iroquois County is a county located in the northeast part of the U.S. state of Illinois. According to the 2020 United States Census, it has a population of 27,077.
It is the only county in the United States named Iroquois. The county seat is Watseka. The county is located along the border with Indiana.

co-58-17031-912.title: Cook County, Illinois
co-58-17031-912.summary: Cook County is the most populous county in the U.S. state of Illinois and the second-most-populous county in the United States, after Los Angeles County, California. More than 40 percent of all residents of Illinois live within Cook County. As of 2020, the population was 5,275,541. The county seat is Chicago, the most populous city in Illinois and the third most populous city in the United States. The county is at the center of the Chicago metropolitan area.

themes.overture: This is a journey up the spine of the Great Migration, tracing the iconic Illinois Central route from the alluvial plains of the Mississippi Delta—the heart of the Blues and the Black Belt—north across the great American watershed divides into the industrial heartland of Chicago.

theses.name: The Migration's Spine
theses.thesis: The leg's route is a physical and cultural transect of the Great Migration, connecting the rural, agricultural Black Belt of Mississippi with the industrial promise and musical legacy of Memphis and Chicago.
anchored_in: Black Belt in the American South

theses.name: Written in Silt
theses.thesis: The entire human story, from Native American settlement to the cotton economy and modern transportation, is built upon a geological canvas of river-deposited sediments, loess, and alluvium left by the Mississippi River system.
anchored_in: Mississippi placenames of Native American origin

theses.name: Haunted Ground
theses.thesis: The landscape is haunted by a history of racial violence and labor struggle, with the ghosts of Emmett Till, the Civil War, and industrial strife embedded in the very towns and fields the train passes.

theses.name: Corridor of Movement
theses.thesis: This route reveals a layered history of American transportation, where the dominant railroad corridor is superimposed on older riverine paths and paralleled by early military airfields and modern auto infrastructure.
anchored_in: United States Army Air Forces Contract Flying School Airfields

movements.at: The crossing of the Ohio River at Cairo, Illinois.
movements.why: This is the journey's great pivot, crossing the historic and geographic boundary between the Deep South and the Midwest, leaving the Lower Mississippi watershed for the Ohio, and traversing a profound dividing line in American history.

movements.at: The transition from the Interior River Valleys and Hills to the Central Corn Belt Plains.
movements.why: The landscape undergoes its final transformation, shifting from the rolling, river-carved topography of the border states to the vast, engineered agricultural grid of the northern Midwest, setting the stage for the industrial metropolis ahead.

movements.at: The continental divide between the Mississippi River and Great Lakes watersheds.
movements.why: An invisible but profound climax, this threshold marks the final departure from the vast hydrological empire of the Mississippi, whose story has defined the entire journey, and the entry into the separate world of the Great Lakes just on the cusp of Chicago.
